## Frequently asked questions
### Is prop money legal to buy and use in Australia?
Yes. Prop currency is completely legal to purchase and use in Australia for legitimate motion picture, television, theatrical, commercial, and training productions provided it adheres to the Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 and Reserve Bank of Australia reproduction guidelines, featuring prominent non-negotiable reproduction markings.

### Can this prop money be spent or circulated as legal tender?
Absolutely not. PROPPS PTY LTD reproduction currency is strictly non-legal tender. Attempting to spend, circulate, or deceive any person or machine with prop currency is a severe criminal offence under Commonwealth law carrying substantial prison penalties.

### What materials are used for your Australian prop banknotes?
Our prop currency is printed on specialized 120gsm high-grade matte archival paper rather than polymer film. This matte finish prevents studio camera reflections, handles realistically during counting scenes, and ensures clear distinction from genuine legal currency.

### What is the minimum order requirement and shipping cost?
Our minimum order value is $300 AUD. Orders of $500 AUD and above qualify for free Australia-wide express shipping. Orders below $500 incur a flat $20 AUD Australia Post Express shipping fee with mandatory signature on delivery.

### How does the 10% cryptocurrency discount work?
When selecting cryptocurrency payment (Bitcoin, USDT TRC20, or Ethereum), a 10% discount is automatically deducted from your order subtotal. You will receive transfer instructions and can confirm your transaction with a TXID.

### Do you offer bulk wholesale pricing for film production studios?
Yes. We supply major streaming studios, theatre companies, escape rooms, and financial training institutions across Australia with custom bulk quantities, specialised serial numbers, and custom vault bricks with tiered wholesale discounts.

### Where are you based and how fast is dispatch?
We are based in Melbourne, Victoria (Eltham, VIC 3093). All orders are packaged discreetly in tamper-evident security boxes and dispatched via Express Australia Post within 24 business hours of payment confirmation.

## Guides
### Ready Prop Money: Stacks That Arrive Set-Ready for Fast Turnarounds
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/ready-prop-money-stacks-for-fast-turnaround/
- Published: 2026-10-10

Call sheets change. A scene moves a day earlier, a table spread becomes a vault reveal, or the director adds a second take of a handover with a different bag. When cash is in the shot, the art department is the department that feels it first. Ready prop money, meaning stacks that are already counted, strapped and sized, takes the preparation out of a late change. This guide explains what ready stacks are, when they save time, how to size and store them, and how to order them for a fast turnaround. Every note we sell is a specimen-marked, non-legal tender prop.

## The short answer

Ready prop money is supplied as pre-counted, strapped stacks, so the art department can place them instead of building them. It saves prep hours, keeps stacks matching across set-ups and makes late changes manageable. Orders dispatch from our Melbourne studio by Australia Post Express, with a signature required on delivery. Browse the [Money Stacks category](/shop/money-stacks/) to see what is available.

## What ready stacks are

A ready stack is a bundle of notes that has been counted and strapped at the studio. The art department opens the box, checks the count and places the stack. Nothing needs to be banded, squared or counted on the morning of the shoot. Stack sizes are standard, so you can plan around them. Our stack tiers run from a Starter Stack through 1, 5, 10, 50 and 100 stacks, which covers anything from a wallet shot to a full vault.

## Why ready stacks help on a tight schedule

1. Less prep. There is no counting or banding on the day. A prop master with a small team can dress a scene in minutes instead of an hour.
2. Consistent look. Matching stacks make continuity simpler between takes and between set-ups.
3. Fewer mistakes. A strapped stack has a known count, so you can track it in and out at the end of the day.
4. Easier handover. The second unit or a new art department assistant can pick up the stacks and place them without a briefing.
5. Faster dispatch. Orders leave our Melbourne studio by Express Post within 24 business hours of payment.

## When ready stacks matter most

Ready stacks pay off whenever time is the scarcest resource:

- Late scene changes. A move from a table spread to a vault reveal needs more stacks, not more preparation.
- Multi-camera days. Two cameras and three set-ups need identical stacks in several places at once.
- Series work. Episode six has to match episode one. Order once, and use the same size and strapping throughout.
- Small crews. Student films and independent productions rarely have a spare person to count and band notes.
- Photography. A studio shoot with an hourly rate benefits from stacks that go straight on the set.

For a longer look at how to match volume to scene, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) and [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/).

## How to size a ready-stack order

Use a simple process:

1. Count the visible stacks. Walk the shot list and count how many stacks the camera sees in each scene.
2. Add the hidden ones. Add stacks that sit behind hero bundles, under bags or in the background. The lens may blur them, but they still need to be there.
3. Allow for continuity. If the same money appears twice in a scene, double the count for the second set-up.
4. Add a reserve. Keep one stack unopened as a spare for late changes.
5. Round up to the nearest tier. The tiers are Starter ($115), 1 Stack ($200), 5 Stacks ($850), 10 Stacks ($1,600), 50 Stacks ($7,500) and 100 Stacks ($14,000), in AUD.

Orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. For larger or repeat runs, ask about wholesale rates on our [wholesale page](/wholesale/).

## Choosing denominations for ready stacks

Ready stacks work best when the denomination mix fits the scene. Use $100 and $50 notes on the visible faces of hero stacks, because those colours read strongly on camera. Add $20, $10 and $5 stacks for tills, wallets and counters. See our [$100 bundle size guide](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) for how to size the biggest stacks, and the guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) for the mix.

## A worked example: a three-day shoot

Imagine a short drama with a bank scene on day one, a car handover on day two and a kitchen-table scene on day three, all using the same money. The art department needs hero stacks for the bank counter, a bag for the car and a close-up bundle for the table.

With ready stacks the plan is simple. Order 5 Stacks for the bank counter and drawer, add a 1 Stack and a Starter Stack for the handover and the table, and keep one stack sealed as a reserve. Because every stack is strapped and counted, the prop master can reset the bag between takes in a minute, track the count at wrap each day and hand the same stacks to the next location. Without ready stacks, each of those resets means banding, squaring and counting by hand while the crew waits.

## Common mistakes with ready stacks

- Opening everything on day one. Keep the reserve sealed until it is needed.
- Ordering different sizes for the same scene. Matching stacks protect continuity, so keep sizes consistent across a scene.
- Not counting at wrap. A quick count at the end of the day is the cheapest way to avoid a missing-stack surprise.
- Leaving the notes unattended. Assign one person and a secure place before the parcel arrives.
- Waiting until the night before. Ready stacks are fast, but a signature is required on delivery and weekends and remote addresses take longer.

## Storing and handling ready stacks on set

A stack that is ready to place should stay that way. A few simple rules keep the notes in good shape and keep the paperwork clean:

- Keep them in the box until the scene. A strap protects the edges and keeps the count.
- Assign one person. The prop master or art department assistant is responsible for the notes, in and out, each day.
- Count at wrap. A quick count at the end of the day catches anything missing before it leaves the location.
- Keep one stack sealed. A reserve for late changes is cheaper than a rush order.
- Protect from moisture and heat. Archival paper handles normally, but damp conditions and hot cars curl edges.
- Never leave notes in a car or on a location overnight. Store them securely.

## Ordering for a fast turnaround

The fastest way to get ready stacks on set is to plan the order a few days before the shoot:

1. Choose your stack tiers and denominations in the [Money Stacks category](/shop/money-stacks/).
2. Place the order and pay at checkout. If you pay in crypto, the 10% discount applies.
3. Orders dispatch from Melbourne by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express within 24 business hours of payment.
4. A signature is required on delivery, so make sure someone is at the address.
5. On arrival, check the count, file the invoice and store the stacks with the prop master.

If your shoot date is very close, [contact the studio](/contact/) and we will tell you what is realistic for your state. Our guide to [shipping and dispatch](/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/) shows typical timings.

## Compliance and responsible use

Ready stacks are still props. Every note carries permanent specimen markings, and every product is a non-legal tender reproduction made for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. They must never be spent, handed out as gifts or tips, or presented as real cash. Keep the invoice on the production file, control the notes on set and brief the cast and crew. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and visit the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the full standard.

### 100 Dollar Prop Money: Which Bundle Size Suits Which Scene
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/
- Published: 2026-10-09

For most Australian productions, 100 dollar prop money does the heavy lifting. The denomination reads clearly on camera, signals value at a glance and holds its colour under both natural and studio light. The harder question is how much to order. Too little and the scene looks thin. Too much and the budget goes on bundles the lens never sees. This guide shows how to pick a bundle size for wallet shots, desk spreads, bag reveals and vault scenes, with the real stack sizes and prices, and a few tricks that let a small order read as a large one. All our notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Match the stack size to what the camera actually sees. A hand or wallet shot needs a Starter Stack. A desk or table spread needs one or two stacks. A bag or briefcase scene needs five. A vault or heist reveal needs ten or more, and a full bank vault scene is where 50 and 100 stack orders come in. Use hero stacks of $100 notes where the camera is close, and fill the rest of the frame with cheaper material.

## The bundle sizes and what they cost

Every product in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) is sold in the same stack tiers. Stack sizes are described by face value, and prices are in AUD:

- Starter Stack: $1,500 face value, $115
- 1 Stack: $2,000 face value, $200
- 5 Stacks: $10,000 face value, $850
- 10 Stacks: $20,000 face value, $1,600
- 50 Stacks: $100,000 face value, $7,500
- 100 Stacks: $200,000 face value, $14,000

Orders start at $300 AUD, so a Starter Stack on its own does not clear the minimum. A Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack, or a single 5 Stacks order, is the usual way to start. Delivery is free from $500 AUD, and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. You can see the current prices on the [$100 product page](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/).

## Match the bundle to the shot

### Wallet or hand shot

A close shot of a hand counting notes or a wallet opening only shows a few notes. One Starter Stack covers it, with plenty left over for continuity. Spend the saved budget on a clean, uncreased hero note that you keep for the close-up.

### Table spread or desk scene

A pile on a table, a desk or a car bonnet needs volume without depth. One or two stacks give a natural-looking spread. Let the notes fall loosely and vary the angles. A neat grid looks staged.

### Bag, briefcase or handover

A handover scene shows a bag opening and a thick bundle at the top. Five stacks usually fill a briefcase to the lip. Put $100 notes on top of the bundles that show, and place filler underneath. If the scene shows the same bag twice, order enough matching stacks so you are not rebuilding them between set-ups.

### Heist or vault reveal

A vault, a safe or a cash room is where the camera pulls back. This is where 10 stacks and above come in. Count the shelves, the pallets and the bags in the frame, then work out how many bundles each one holds. For the biggest scenes our [Money Stacks category](/shop/money-stacks/) and [wholesale page](/wholesale/) are the right place to start. Our guide to [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/) goes through the maths in detail.

## Make a small order look big

Art departments rarely buy a full vault of hero notes. These are the usual tricks:

1. Hero on top, filler underneath. The camera sees the top note and the stack edges. Put $100 notes at the visible faces and cheaper material behind them.
2. Fan the notes. A fanned handful reads as a thicker stack than a flat one.
3. Vary the denominations. An all-$100 drawer looks wrong. Mix in $50 and $20 notes, as our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) explains.
4. Use depth of field. A shallow focus blurs bundles in the background, so you do not need hero quality there.
5. Break the line. Open a strap, spill a few notes and leave one stack at an angle. Perfect order looks fake.
6. Keep spares. Hold one stack unopened as a reserve for late changes.

## Continuity and re-takes

Continuity is the quiet cost of a cash scene. If the same money appears before and after a handover, you need matching stacks for both sides of the cut. Notes are double-sided, so a flipped stack still looks right. Order the full quantity for a block of shooting in one go, so the notes in scene 12 match the notes in scene 3. If you need a repeat order, [contact the studio](/contact/) and mention the earlier order.

## Worked examples

These three examples show how the same tiers stretch across different scenes. Quantities are a starting point. Always count what your own shot list shows.

### A bank counter scene

The camera starts on a teller counting a bundle, then cuts to a wide of the counter with a few stacks. One 5 Stacks order covers the hero stacks, the teller's drawer and a reserve. Put $100 and $50 notes on the visible faces of the bundles and use $20 and $10 notes in the drawer. Total: $850, which also clears the order minimum and delivery threshold.

### A kitchen-table handover

A character slides a bundle across a table, and the camera holds on the money for two seconds. One stack in a close-up is enough, and a Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack ($315 together) clears the minimum with room for a second take and a reserve. If the scene is shot twice from different angles, the second stack lets the art department reset instantly without rebuilding the first.

### A vault reveal

A heist or security scene pulls back to show shelves of bundles. A 10 Stacks order ($1,600) fills a modest vault. A larger set with pallets and open bags suits 50 Stacks ($7,500). A full cash room is where 100 Stacks ($14,000) and a wholesale conversation make sense. In every case, put hero stacks at the front and let depth of field handle the back.

## Common mistakes with bundle sizes

- Ordering for the whole frame instead of the visible faces. The camera sees the top of a stack, not its core.
- Forgetting the second set-up. Matching stacks for a second angle save more time than they cost.
- Buying only $100 notes. A drawer or wallet with a single denomination looks staged.
- No reserve. A single unopened stack is cheaper than a rush order on the morning of the shoot.
- Leaving it late. Express dispatch is fast, but it needs someone at the address to sign.

## Why $100 notes dominate screen work

The Reserve Bank's current $100 note is a strong, saturated green that reads on camera under most lighting, and the denomination signals value instantly. That is why productions lean on $100 and $50 notes for hero stacks and use $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills, wallets and counters. If you are choosing between denominations, read our [guide to the $50 and $100 range](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) and browse the [$50 product](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) alongside the $100.

## Compliance and handling

Every note carries permanent specimen markings, and every product is a non-legal tender reproduction made for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Keep the notes with the prop master, count them in and out each day, keep the invoice on file and never spend them or hand them out. For the legal background read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and visit the [compliance page](/compliance/). The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes its own guidance on banknote reproductions.

### High Quality Prop Money: How to Judge It Before Your Shoot
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/high-quality-prop-money-how-to-judge-it-on-camera/
- Published: 2026-10-07

High quality prop money is easy to spot once you know what to look for, and just as easy to miss if you judge it from a product photo. A render can hide soft print, glare-prone paper and edges that curl after two takes. This guide gives you a practical way to judge prop money before your shoot: four checks for the notes themselves, tests you can run under your own lights, questions to put to a supplier and the red flags that tell you to walk away. It is written for art departments, photographers and directors. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Judge prop money on four things: print detail, paper, double-sided finish and handling. Then test a sample under the lighting you will actually use, both at arm's length and up close. Quality is not about looking identical to a real banknote. It is about reading correctly on camera while staying clearly marked and different in the hand.

## Check 1: Print detail

Fine line work is the first thing to fail in a cheap print. Hold a note at arm's length: the main design, portrait and colour blocks should look clean. Then bring it close: fine lines should stay crisp rather than turning into a blur or showing visible dots. If you are shooting a close-up of a hand counting notes, the lens will see the fine detail. If the print softens at your working distance, it will soften on camera.

Look at colour as well as detail. Saturated colourways such as the gold of the $50 and the green of the $100 should read as deep, even colours, not flat or patchy. Check that the colours match across a stack, because two print runs that do not match are a continuity problem.

## Check 2: Paper

Paper decides how a note behaves under lights. A glossy or reflective stock throws hot spots into the lens, and a thin stock looks flimsy as soon as an actor handles it. Matte, non-reflective stock handles naturally and avoids glare under studio lighting. PROPPS notes are printed on 120gsm archival paper, which is heavy enough to feel like a note and matte enough to stay out of trouble with a lighting rig. Our guide to [lighting prop money on camera without glare](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) goes through the lighting side.

Paper also matters for compliance. Genuine Australian banknotes are polymer, so a reproduction on paper is easy to tell apart by touch. That is a deliberate feature, not a compromise.

## Check 3: Both sides

Many cheap prints are one-sided or have a rough reverse. That matters whenever an actor fans, flips or counts notes, because the camera will see the back. Check that both sides carry the same print quality, and that the reverse is aligned with the front. Our notes are printed double-sided, so a fanned or flipped stack looks right.

## Check 4: Handling

A scene may need ten takes. Notes should survive repeated handling without curling, creasing badly or tearing. Test a sample note by folding it once, fanning it and counting it through your fingers a dozen times. Look at the corners and edges. If the corners round off or the edges fray in a few minutes, the notes will not last a day on set.

## A simple on-set test

Before you commit to a large order, run this five-minute test with a sample:

1. Light it as you will shoot it. Use your actual key light, practicals and any bounce.
2. Check at working distance. View the note through the lens or monitor at the distance of your wide, medium and close shots.
3. Tilt it. Rotate the note slowly and watch for hot spots and reflections.
4. Handle it. Fan, flip, count and fold it a dozen times.
5. Compare to your other props. Put it next to the wallet, the bag or the desk it will sit on.
6. Take photos on the camera you will use. The monitor lies less than a product page does.

## Questions to ask a supplier

Good suppliers answer these directly. Evasive answers are a warning.

1. Can I see a close-up photo of an actual note, front and back?
2. What is the paper stock and weight?
3. Are the notes printed on both sides?
4. Are the specimen markings permanent, and where are they?
5. Can I order a sample or see a hand-held video?
6. How are the notes counted and strapped?
7. Do I get an invoice and written product description for the production file?
8. How is the order delivered, and is a signature required?

## Red flags

Quality and honesty tend to travel together. Walk away if you see:

- Renders instead of photos. If every image is a mock-up, the real product may not match.
- No specimen markings. Unmarked notes are the biggest risk for buyers.
- Claims of undetectable quality or passing tests. That is the wrong promise for a prop.
- Government clearance claims with no source. Regulators do not approve individual prop sellers.
- Unmarked or discreet packaging as a selling point. Legitimate props do not need to hide.
- No Australian business details. You should be able to see an ABN and an address.

For more on weighing up suppliers, read [where to buy prop money in Australia legally](/blog/where-to-buy-prop-money-in-australia-legally/) and [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/).

## What quality means for different shoots

The same note is judged differently depending on the job:

- A feature film close-up needs crisp fine detail, accurate colour and a natural feel in the actor's hand. Judge the note at working distance and check both sides.
- A television drama often shoots fast with multiple set-ups, so handling and matching stacks matter as much as print detail.
- Theatre is viewed from a distance, so colour and durability matter more than the finest line work. Notes get handled every night.
- Photography shows everything at high resolution and under controlled lighting, so paper finish and glare control matter most. Read our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).
- Content creators shoot on phones and small cameras, where bright, saturated colour and clear markings read well. See the [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/).

## Keeping prop money in good condition

Even good notes can be ruined by poor storage. Keep them flat, dry and out of direct sun. Avoid leaving them in a hot car, where edges curl. Keep them strapped and in the box until the scene. Handle them by the edges, and keep a few spare notes for hero shots so the best ones are not handled more than needed. At wrap, count the notes in and store them with the prop master, never loose in a bag or costume.

## Quality is not the same as cost

A higher price does not guarantee quality, and a low price does not always mean poor quality. What matters is whether the price covers the things you cannot see on a product page: paper weight, double-sided alignment, consistent colour between runs, counting and strapping, paperwork and delivery. Our guide to [cheap prop money and what you are really paying for](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) goes through the trade-offs. At PROPPS, orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount.

## Match quality to the shot

Not every shot needs the same level of detail. A close-up of a hand counting notes needs hero-quality print and handling. A wide of a vault needs volume, and a shallow depth of field will blur the bundles at the back. Put your best notes where the camera is close and use stacks for the rest. Our guide to [$100 prop money bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) shows how to split an order between hero and background stacks.

## Compliance still matters

High quality does not mean realistic enough to deceive. Every note we sell carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender prop for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Keep the notes under the prop master's control, never spend them and never post unmarked close-ups that suggest the cash is real. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and visit the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the full standard.

### Cheap Prop Money: What You Are Really Paying For (and What You Give Up)
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/
- Published: 2026-10-06

Everyone wants a good price, and prop money is no exception. A listing that says cheap prop money looks like a bargain, especially on a small budget. Sometimes it is. Often the saving is paid for somewhere you cannot see on a product page: in the paper, the print, the markings, the paperwork or the delivery. This guide explains what drives the price of prop money, where cheap listings cut corners, when cheap is fine, when it is not and how to get a fair price without taking a risk. It is written for art departments, producers, photographers and event hosts. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Cheap prop money is fine for the far background of a shot and for casual events. For anything the camera sees closely, or anything that needs paperwork, the saving usually costs more than it saves. Judge a price against what is included: markings, paper, print quality, counting, strapping, invoice and traceable delivery.

## What drives the price of prop money

Seven things set the price of a stack of notes.

1. Paper. Heavier matte archival paper costs more than thin gloss stock. PROPPS uses 120gsm matte archival paper.
2. Print quality. Crisp fine print, accurate colour and consistent runs cost more than a basic print.
3. Double-sided alignment. Both sides aligned and matched takes care.
4. Specimen markings. Permanent, prominent markings are part of the design and the compliance standard.
5. Counting and strapping. A counted, strapped stack saves art department time.
6. Paperwork. An invoice and a written description for the production file.
7. Delivery. Traceable, signed-for shipping costs more than a postage stamp.

## Where cheap listings cut corners

Here are the places a low price usually comes from.

- Thin or glossy paper. It reflects light, curls and feels cheap in the hand.
- Soft or off-colour print. It looks fine in a thumbnail and poor at working distance.
- One-sided or misaligned prints. A flipped note shows a blank or a blurred back.
- Weak or missing markings. This is the biggest risk, because markings are what make a note a prop.
- No counting. Loose notes mean prep time and uncertain quantities.
- No invoice. You have nothing for the production file.
- Slow, untracked delivery. You cannot plan around it.
- Overseas origin. Polymer copies of Australian designs, weak markings and border delays. See [local vs overseas suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/).

## The real cost of a cheap order

A low price can turn into a higher cost.

- Rework. If the notes look wrong on camera, you reorder or reshoot.
- Rush fees. A late replacement costs more than the original.
- Lost time. Counting, banding and sorting loose notes takes crew hours.
- Compliance risk. Notes without clear markings can cause problems with venues, insurers or police.
- No recourse. If the order is wrong, you may have nobody to contact.

## When cheap is fine

There are good uses for lower-cost notes.

1. The far background. A bundle at the back of a shelf that the lens will blur.
2. Casual events. A party where play money is the right choice. See [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/).
3. Rehearsals and tests. A cheap stack for blocking and testing light.
4. Filler. Stock beneath hero notes in a bag or a stack.

## When cheap is a bad idea

Avoid low-cost notes for:

- Close-ups and inserts. The camera sees the print and the paper.
- Hero stacks. These carry the scene.
- Public shoots. You need marked notes and paperwork.
- Anything that will be published. A weak note shows in a still.
- Repeat orders. You need matching stock.

## How to get a fair price

Good value is not the same as the lowest price. These steps help.

1. Size the order properly. Do not buy more than the camera sees. Our guide to [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) shows how.
2. Put hero quality where the camera is close. Use matching stock behind it.
3. Order once. One order saves minimums, shipping and mismatches.
4. Ask about wholesale tiers. Larger and repeat runs may be 10% to 30% off. See the [wholesale page](/wholesale/).
5. Use the crypto discount if it suits you. PROPPS gives 10% off crypto payments.
6. Reuse stacks across scenes. Matching stacks can appear more than once.

## What PROPPS prices look like

At PROPPS, orders start at $300 AUD and delivery is free from $500 AUD. Stacks run from $115 for a Starter Stack to $14,000 for 100 Stacks. Every note is specimen-marked, printed double-sided on matte archival paper and sold with an invoice. Our guide to [high quality prop money](/blog/high-quality-prop-money-how-to-judge-it-on-camera/) shows what to check in any listing.

## A quick price check

Before you buy from anyone, ask:

1. Can I see a photo of an actual note, front and back?
2. Is the specimen marking on every note?
3. What is the paper?
4. Are the stacks counted and strapped?
5. Will I get an invoice?
6. How is it delivered, and is a signature required?
7. Can I reorder matching stock?

If a seller dodges these, the low price is telling you something.

## Compliance

Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Never spend them. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [Reserve Bank guidance](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/).

## A worked comparison

Imagine two quotes for the same scene. The first is a low-cost listing: thin glossy notes, loose in a bag, one-sided print, no invoice, delivered in three weeks. The second is a local studio order: matte double-sided notes, counted and strapped, specimen-marked, with an invoice and signed-for delivery in days. The first looks cheaper. Then add the crew hours to count and band the notes, the cost of replacing notes that read badly on camera, the rush delivery for a missed date and the lack of paperwork. The second is often the cheaper job overall, and it carries far less risk.

## Hidden costs to watch for

- Minimum order and shipping. A low unit price with a high postage fee is not a bargain.
- Currency conversion. An overseas price in another currency moves with the exchange rate.
- Customs and handling. Charges can appear on arrival.
- Time. Slow delivery can force a rush order elsewhere.
- Quality drift. A repeat order may not match the first.

## Cheap play money versus cheap prop money

The cheapest option for a party or a classroom is often play money, which is designed to look unlike real notes and costs far less to make. That is a good choice for games. It is not a substitute for prop money in a close-up. If your budget is tight and your shot is a wide, play money in the background and a small hero stack of marked notes in the foreground is a sensible split. Our [play money vs prop money guide](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) shows how to choose.

## Saving money by planning

The most reliable way to cut cost is not a cheaper note but a better plan. Count what the camera sees, reuse stacks across scenes, weather only what is handled and order once. Our guides to [how much prop money you need](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) and [heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/) show how a small order can look large on screen. A good plan can cut the quantity by a third without the audience noticing.

## What to ask for before you accept a low price

If a low price tempts you, ask for a photo of an actual note, a description of the paper, confirmation that the markings are on every note, the delivery method and an invoice. A seller who answers clearly and quickly has probably earned the price. A seller who avoids the questions has probably cut the corners you cannot see. Check before you pay, because refunds from distant sellers are slow, and a missed shoot cannot be undone.

## A budget-friendly plan that still looks right

Spend on the notes the camera sees closely: the hero stack, the fan, the insert. Use matching but simpler stock for the background. Weather only what is handled, and reuse stacks between set-ups. Order once, keep a reserve and ask about tiers. That plan keeps the cost down and the screen quality up, without leaning on the cheapest listing you can find.

### Is It Illegal to Buy Prop Money in Australia? The Plain-English Answer
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/is-it-illegal-to-buy-prop-money-australia/
- Published: 2026-10-05

Is it illegal to buy prop money in Australia? In most cases, no. Buying clearly marked reproduction notes for a film, a stage show, a photo shoot or a training exercise is a normal business purchase. What is illegal is making, using or passing off notes that could deceive someone into accepting them as real money. This guide separates the two, explains the situations where people get into trouble, and gives you a plain checklist. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

Buying prop money is lawful when the notes are clearly marked as reproductions, differ from genuine notes, and are bought for a legitimate purpose. The risk comes from what happens after the purchase: spending prop notes, presenting them as real, removing the markings or buying notes that were never marked in the first place. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) is the law that applies, and Section 22 is the provision our compliance standard is built around.

## Buying, using and making are three different things

Most confusion comes from treating these as one question.

- Buying marked reproduction notes from a local supplier for production use is routine.
- Using them means handling them on set, in a studio or in a training room. That is lawful when the notes are marked, controlled and not offered as payment.
- Making reproductions yourself is where people fall into trouble, because a home-printed note that looks convincing has none of the safeguards a professional studio builds in. Do not make your own.

## What keeps a prop lawful

Three things carry most of the weight, and a supplier should be able to show you each of them.

1. It is marked. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings in line with Section 22 and the Reserve Bank's reproduction guidance.
2. It is different. Real Australian banknotes are polymer. Our reproductions are printed on non-reflective archival paper, so they are easy to tell apart by touch.
3. It is honestly sold. The product description states that the notes are non-legal tender props made for film, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training.

Read more about how this works in our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and on our [compliance page](/compliance/).

## Situations that cause problems

The notes are rarely the problem. The situations around them are.

- Spending a prop note. Handing a prop note to a shop, a taxi driver or an ATM, even as a joke, is the fastest route to a police report.
- Pranks and stunts. A video of someone "paying" with prop cash can be treated as an attempt to deceive, whatever the caption says.
- Covering the markings. Removing, cropping or hiding the specimen markings changes the legal position of the notes.
- Buying unmarked notes. Notes with no markings, or with markings so faint they are easy to miss, are the main cause of trouble for buyers.
- Careless storage. Loose prop notes left in a car, a costume pocket or a rental can end up in the wrong hands.
- Cash giveaways. Content that suggests real cash is being given away, using prop notes, can mislead viewers and attract complaints.

## Shooting in public places

If your scene is shot in a street, shop or bank, tell the venue or local police beforehand and keep the supplier's invoice on set. Staff and members of the public cannot tell what is a prop from a distance. A short written note from the production company and a call to the local station can prevent a long afternoon.

Two further habits help. First, keep notes under the prop master's control and count them in and out each shooting day. Second, never let background performers keep souvenir notes. Even a single marked note in a wallet can turn into a question that nobody wants to answer.

## What if you are asked about a prop note?

Stay calm and show the markings. Explain that the note is a reproduction made for production use and show the supplier invoice. If you are speaking to police, it is reasonable to offer the supplier's details and the production file. Buying from a local, ABN-registered studio makes this simple. Overseas sellers on marketplace sites usually cannot supply any of it. For concerns about counterfeit currency, the [Australian Federal Police](https://www.afp.gov.au/) is the point of contact.

## Crossing borders with prop money

Carrying prop notes into or out of Australia raises extra questions. Customs officers see a bundle of banknote-like paper and have to decide what it is. Declare the notes, carry the invoice and keep the markings visible. If you are travelling for a shoot, ask the production's customs broker or legal adviser before you pack. Shipping from a local supplier with traceable dispatch is almost always simpler than carrying notes in luggage. Read about our [shipping and dispatch](/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/) options.

## What insurers and location owners usually ask for

Insurers and location owners are not lawyers, and they rarely ask for legal analysis. They want to know three things: what the notes are, who supplied them and who is responsible for them. A short file covers all three:

- The supplier's invoice, with the business name, ABN and address.
- A photo of the front and back of a note, showing the specimen markings.
- A line in the call sheet or prop schedule naming the scene and the person in charge of the notes.

Bring the same file to any public location shoot. It turns a long conversation with a nervous venue manager into a short one.

## Common myths

"It is only illegal if you spend it." Spending is the clearest problem, but removing the markings, presenting prop cash as real or buying unmarked notes also create risk.

"Prop money is illegal everywhere." It is not. Marked reproductions are a normal supply item in the Australian film, theatre and photography industries.

"A home-printed note is cheaper and just as safe." It is neither. A home-printed copy has no specimen markings and no supplier paperwork, and a convincing copy is exactly what the law is written to catch.

## Why we publish this guide

PROPPS PTY LTD supplies prop currency to Australian productions, and the question we hear most often is whether the purchase itself is a problem. We would rather answer it plainly on a public page than leave buyers to guess from forum posts or from sellers who have a reason to say "no problem at all". If you read nothing else, remember the order of operations: buy marked notes from a supplier you can identify, keep the paperwork, control the notes on set and never offer them as payment.

## Is it illegal to buy play money or party money?

Buying play money, toy money or novelty party notes is not illegal. They are designed to look nothing like real currency. If you want something a little more realistic for a themed event, choose marked notes from a local supplier and keep them out of circulation. Our [novelty money guide](/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/) and [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit that use.

## A practical checklist before you buy

1. Confirm the notes carry permanent specimen markings, and ask for a photo of the front and back.
2. Buy from an Australian business with an ABN and a physical address.
3. Check the notes are paper, not polymer.
4. Make sure the product page states the notes are non-legal tender props.
5. Choose signed-for delivery.
6. File the invoice and a note of the production use.
7. Brief everyone who will touch the notes: never spend them, show them off as real cash or post unmarked close-ups.

If you want to know whether you can buy prop money in the first place, read [can you buy prop money in Australia](/blog/can-you-buy-prop-money-in-australia/). This article is general information, not legal advice. Check the current Act, the RBA's guidance and your own legal adviser for a specific production.

### Can You Buy Prop Money in Australia? What You Can Order and What to Check
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/can-you-buy-prop-money-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-10-04

Can you buy prop money in Australia? Yes. Production companies, photographers, theatres, advertising agencies and training providers buy marked reproduction notes every week. The legal point is not whether you can buy them but what you are buying and what you do with it. This guide explains who buys prop money, what a legitimate order looks like, how to check a supplier, what it costs and how to place an order, in plain English. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

You can buy prop money in Australia from a local supplier when the notes are clearly marked as reproductions, differ from genuine notes in material and treatment, and are sold for legitimate purposes. You cannot use prop money as payment, and you should not buy notes that are marketed as spendable, undetectable or "real looking" with no markings. Our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains the law behind that line.

## Who buys prop money

Prop money has a surprisingly wide customer base. The most common buyers are:

- Film and television productions: art departments dressing bank, casino, crime and street scenes.
- Theatre companies: stage cash that reads from the back row without needing to be genuine.
- Photographers and content studios: lifestyle, fashion and advertising shoots where cash is a visual element.
- Advertising and event agencies: branded prop currency for campaigns and launches.
- Training providers: cash-handling and security exercises where real money is not appropriate.
- Event organisers: parties, fundraisers and casino nights, where marked novelty notes are enough.

Different buyers need different things. A feature film needs hundreds of notes in realistic bundles. A party host needs a few marked stacks. Our [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) covers the five denominations used on screen, and our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit lighter use.

## What a legitimate order looks like

A lawful order has four features, and you can check all four before you pay:

1. Visible specimen markings on every note. Ask for a photo of the front and back. The marking should be permanent and prominent, not a faint watermark.
2. A local supplier with an ABN. You can then see who you are paying, get an invoice and contact someone if there is a problem.
3. Paper, not polymer. Real Australian banknotes are polymer. Reproductions on matte paper are easy to tell apart by touch. PROPPS prints on non-reflective archival paper.
4. A clear use. The product page states what the notes are for: film, television, theatre, photography, art or training.

## How to check a prop money supplier

A few minutes of checking separates a studio you can rely on from an anonymous seller:

- Business details. Look for an ABN, a physical address and a working phone number. PROPPS PTY LTD is based in Eltham, Victoria, and has supplied Australian productions since 2019.
- Product descriptions. The copy should say the notes are non-legal tender props. Be wary of any listing that describes them as spendable or able to pass tests.
- Dispatch. Traceable shipping with a signature is a good sign. Offers of "discreet" or unmarked packaging are a bad one.
- Track record. Look for named productions, a physical studio, policies for returns and shipping, and a compliance page that quotes the law accurately.
- Overseas marketplaces. Listings that ship polymer notes copying current Australian designs sit close to the legal line and can be stopped at the border. Our guide to [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/) compares the options.

Prices vary with note count, denomination and how closely the finish matches the shot you need. Stack products are sized by face value, so you can scale from a single hero stack to a full bank vault.

A few rules of thumb:

- A single scene with one hero stack is usually covered by the minimum order.
- A bank or casino scene needs many bundles but only a few hero notes. Mix quantities to match what the camera sees.
- A season of a series costs less per scene when you order once, which is what our [wholesale page](/wholesale/) is for.

For more on matching volume to the shot, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) and [cheap prop money and what you are really paying for](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/).

## How to order, step by step

1. Decide the use. Write down the scene, the denominations and roughly how many bundles are visible.
2. Pick the notes. Start with the [$100](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) and [$50](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) products, which dominate Australian screen work, and add smaller denominations for tills and wallets.

## Choosing denominations and bundle sizes

Australian screen work leans on the $50 and $100 notes because their colours read strongly on camera, but a believable cash scene usually mixes denominations. Use $100 and $50 notes for hero stacks and close-ups. Add $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills, wallets and counter exchanges, where an all-$100 drawer would look wrong. Our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) shows how to split a budget across them.

Bundle size matters as much as denomination. The camera sees the top note and the edges of a stack, so a heavy-looking bundle does not always need a heavy order. Many art departments buy a handful of hero stacks and fill the rest of the frame with filler paper behind them. ## Common mistakes when buying prop money

- Ordering from the cheapest listing. A low price often means no markings, no invoice and no one to call. Our guide to [cheap prop money](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) explains where the saving really goes.
- Leaving it to the last week. Express dispatch is fast, but a signature is required, so allow time to arrange someone at the delivery address.
- Forgetting storage. Decide who holds the notes between shooting days before they arrive.
- Skipping the paperwork. An invoice and the marking details take two minutes to file and answer most questions later.

## Buying for a one-off event versus a production

A one-off buyer, such as someone dressing a casino night or a photo shoot, usually needs a small order and no wholesale terms. A production company buying for a series needs consistency between orders, so the notes in episode six match the notes in episode one. If that is you, mention it when you [contact the studio](/contact/), because repeat orders can be planned and priced together. Either way, the legal checklist is the same: marked notes, an Australian supplier, an invoice and signed-for delivery.

## What you cannot do with prop money

Buying is lawful when the notes are marked and the purpose is legitimate. These are not:

- Spending prop notes, even once, as a test or a joke.
- Handing prop notes to anyone as a tip, a gift or a payment.
- Posting close-ups that suggest the cash is real.
- Removing or covering the specimen markings.
- Selling prop notes as genuine currency.

If a police officer or a shop assistant asks about a note, show the specimen marking and the invoice. That is what they are for. The [Australian Federal Police](https://www.afp.gov.au/) is the right contact for concerns about counterfeit currency, and the RBA publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

### Local vs Overseas Prop Money Suppliers: What Australian Productions Should Check
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/
- Published: 2026-09-22

Search for Australian dollar prop notes and the results mix local studios with overseas marketplaces, listings with photos that look the same and prices that differ wildly. The cheapest option is often overseas, and the pitch is simple: the same notes for less. The truth is more complicated. Prop money is a product where the details that matter, such as markings, paper, paperwork and delivery, are the ones a listing hides. This guide compares local and overseas suppliers across the factors that matter to an art department, producer or event host, explains the risks of each and gives you a checklist for choosing. It is general information, not legal advice. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

For film, television, theatre, photography and any job that needs paperwork, buy from a local studio with marked notes, an ABN, signed-for delivery and an invoice. Overseas listings can be cheaper, but they often ship polymer notes that closely copy Australian designs, with weak markings, long delivery, uncertain paperwork and the risk of being held at the border.

## What the two options look like

### Local studio

A local studio is an Australian business that designs, prints and ships prop currency to Australian buyers. PROPPS is one, based in Eltham, Melbourne, supplying Australian productions since 2019. Typical features: specimen markings on every note, matte paper, an ABN, a physical address, an invoice, traceable Express Post delivery and a contact you can call.

### Overseas marketplace

An overseas marketplace listing is a seller, often in another country, who ships prop notes by international post. Typical features: a low price per pack, large minimum quantities, long delivery, polymer notes that match Australian designs closely, weak or missing markings and no local contact.

## Side by side

- Markings. Local: permanent on every note. Overseas: faint, partial or absent.
- Material. Local: matte paper. Overseas: often polymer, which is the same material as real Australian notes.
- Legal position. Local: built to Section 22 and the RBA guidance. Overseas: often unclear.
- Delivery. Local: Australia Post Express in days, with a signature. Overseas: weeks, with customs risk.
- Paperwork. Local: an invoice for the production file. Overseas: a marketplace receipt, if that.
- Recourse. Local: a phone number. Overseas: a message to a seller in another time zone.
- Consistency. Local: matching stock across orders. Overseas: variable.
- Price. Local: higher per note. Overseas: lower, until you add the risks.

## Why polymer copies are the biggest risk

Australian banknotes are printed on polymer. A reproduction that is also polymer and closely copies the design is the kind of item the law is concerned about, because it can feel and look like the real thing. A paper reproduction with permanent markings is easy to tell apart by touch and by eye. That is why PROPPS prints on paper and marks every note. If you buy polymer copies from overseas, you take on the risk that they are held at the border, questioned by a venue or mistaken for real money. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions, and our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains the law in plain English.

## Delivery and timing

A shoot has a date. A local studio dispatches within 24 business hours of payment by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express, and the parcel is tracked and signed for. An overseas order can take weeks, can be held at customs and cannot be rushed. If a scene changes, the local studio can send a new stack. The overseas seller cannot. Our guide to [shipping and dispatch](/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/) explains the local process.

## Paperwork and insurance

Insurers, location owners and police ask what the notes are and where they came from. A local invoice with an ABN, a photo of a marked note and a line in the call sheet answers all three. An overseas marketplace receipt with a seller handle does not. If a question comes up months later, the local paper trail is still there. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) sets out the standard.

## Price: the real comparison

The price on an overseas listing is only part of the cost. Add shipping, customs and handling, the risk of a delay, the cost of a replacement if the notes are wrong and the crew time spent sorting loose notes. A local order at a higher unit price is often the cheaper job overall. Our guide to [cheap prop money](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) goes through the trade-offs, and our [how much prop money guide](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) helps you avoid overbuying.

## A checklist for choosing

1. Specimen markings on every note. Ask for a photo of the front and back of an actual note.
2. Paper, not polymer.
3. Australian business details. ABN, address and phone number.
4. Honest product description. It should say non-legal tender prop.
5. Signed-for, traceable delivery.
6. An invoice.
7. A way to reorder matching stock.
8. A plan for what to do if something is wrong.

## When overseas might make sense

There are cases where an overseas order is reasonable: a small, non-visible background item, a different currency we do not supply, or a very large order where a local quote is out of reach. Even then, check the markings, plan for delays and keep the paperwork. PROPPS makes Australian dollar props only. If you need another currency, a specialist overseas supplier may be the right choice.

## Compliance

Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Never spend them, and keep them under the prop master's control. If you have concerns about counterfeit currency, contact the [Australian Federal Police](https://www.afp.gov.au/).

## Questions to ask any supplier, local or overseas

1. Where are the notes printed, and by whom?
2. Can I see a photo of an actual note, front and back, showing the markings?
3. What is the paper or material?
4. What is the delivery method, and what happens if the parcel is held?
5. Do I get an invoice that names the product?
6. Who do I contact if the count is wrong?
7. Can I reorder matching stock?

Local studios usually answer these in a line or two. Overseas sellers often cannot, or do not.

## A short story to illustrate the risk

Picture a producer who orders a large pack of polymer notes from an overseas marketplace to save money. The parcel is held at the border for weeks, the shoot date passes and a replacement order is placed with a local studio at a rush price. The savings are gone, the schedule slipped and the producer has no paperwork for the first order. The lesson is not that every overseas order fails. It is that the cost of failure is much larger than the saving.

## Supporting local makers

Buying from a local studio keeps jobs and skills in the industry, and it means the supplier understands the Australian rules on reproductions. A local maker is also easier to hold to account. If a note is wrong, a call or a message gets a reply on the same day, not a week later.

## How to switch suppliers safely

If you have used an overseas supplier before, run a small test order with a local studio first. Compare the print, the paper, the markings and the delivery. Check the paperwork. If the test passes, move the whole order across. Keep both invoices on the file for a few months, so you can show the change if anyone asks.

## What local studios should be able to show you

A good local studio can show a photo of a marked note on request, a clear description of the paper, a named business with an ABN, published shipping and refund policies and a recent order history. It can also explain how its notes are built to the Section 22 standard, in plain language. If a studio cannot do these things, keep looking. The same test applies to any overseas seller you consider.

## A final word on risk

Risk is the part of the price that never appears on a listing. A small saving on the unit price can be wiped out by one held parcel, one missed date or one awkward question from a venue. Weigh the whole picture, ask the questions above and choose the supplier you would be comfortable explaining to your producer.

### Shipping and Dispatch: How Fast Can You Get Prop Money in Australia?
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-08-18

When a shoot is booked and the cash scene is on Thursday, the question is not only where to buy prop money but how quickly it can arrive and who needs to be at the door. Searching for prop money near you usually means a deadline. This guide explains how PROPPS dispatches orders from Melbourne, how Australia Post Express and the signature requirement work, what to expect for Melbourne, Sydney and the rest of the country, how to plan delivery around a shoot and what to do if something goes wrong. It is general information. Delivery times depend on Australia Post and the destination, so check their estimates for your address. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

PROPPS dispatches from its Eltham, Melbourne studio within 24 business hours of payment, by Australia Post Express with a mandatory signature on delivery. Orders start at $300 AUD and delivery is free from $500 AUD. Tell the studio your shoot date when you order, nominate someone to sign and allow a few days between order and first use.

## How dispatch works

1. You order and pay. Add items to the cart and pay by bank transfer, PayID or crypto, which receives a 10% discount.
2. We confirm. You receive an invoice and a confirmation.
3. We pack and dispatch. Orders leave the Melbourne studio within 24 business hours of payment.
4. Australia Post Express carries it. The parcel is tracked.
5. Someone signs. A signature is mandatory on delivery. If nobody is there, the parcel goes to a collection point or a redelivery is arranged.
6. You check and file. Count the notes, check the condition and file the invoice.

## Why a signature is required

Every parcel of prop currency ships with a mandatory signature on delivery. That means a named person receives it, the delivery is recorded and the notes do not sit unattended on a doorstep. It protects the production and it protects us. For a shoot, nominate someone who will be at the address, and give their name and a mobile number at checkout. If the address is a location, a production office or a studio, tell the receptionist or the security desk to expect the parcel.

## Melbourne, Sydney and the rest of Australia

PROPPS is based in Eltham, Melbourne, so Melbourne orders have the shortest distance to travel. Sydney, Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth, Hobart, Darwin and Canberra are all served by Express Post, with delivery times set by Australia Post for each route. Regional and remote addresses usually take longer. We cannot promise a specific day for every address, so check [Australia Post's delivery estimates](https://auspost.com.au/) for your postcode, and allow extra time before a fixed shoot date.

## Planning delivery around a shoot

A simple plan avoids stress.

1. Order early. Aim for a few days before the first cash scene, more for regional addresses.
2. Tell us the date. Mention your shoot date when you order, so we can flag it.
3. Choose the address carefully. A production office or a prop room with a person on site is better than a location that moves.
4. Name the signer. Give a name and a mobile number.
5. Plan for a miss. If the first delivery attempt fails, know where the parcel will go and who can collect it.
6. Keep a spare. Have a reserve stack in case a scene changes.

Our [buying checklist for art departments](/blog/buying-film-props-in-australia-a-checklist-for-art-departments/) explains the wider buying process.

## Delivering to a location or hotel

Shoots move. If you are travelling, do not send notes to a hotel unless the hotel can hold and sign for a parcel. A production office, a studio or a trusted contact is a safer address. Never ask for a parcel to be left unattended. If the shoot is interstate, ask the studio about delivering to a local production address ahead of the crew.

## What is in the box

Notes are counted and strapped, packed securely and sent in packaging that protects the edges. An invoice goes with the order or is emailed. The parcel is tracked. We do not offer unmarked or discreet packaging as a feature, because legitimate props do not need to hide, and traceable, signed-for delivery is the safer arrangement for everyone.

## Checking your order on arrival

1. Check the parcel for damage before signing, and note any damage on the delivery receipt.
2. Open it with the person who signed, and count the stacks against the invoice.
3. Check a note front and back for the specimen markings.
4. Photograph the contents and keep the photos with the invoice.
5. Store the notes with the prop master in a secure, dry place.
6. Contact the studio straight away if anything is wrong.

## If something goes wrong

If a parcel is late, check the tracking and contact Australia Post, then let us know. If a delivery is missed, arrange a redelivery or a pickup. If a count is wrong or a note is damaged, tell us with photos on the day of delivery, and we will sort it out. Our [contact page](/contact/) and WhatsApp are the fastest routes.

## Compliance and handling

Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction. Keep the notes under the prop master's control, keep the invoice on file and never spend them. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/), the [compliance page](/compliance/) and the [Reserve Bank guidance](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) for the standard.

## A sample timeline for a Friday shoot

Imagine a cash scene on Friday. Order on Monday, so payment is confirmed early in the week. Dispatch leaves Melbourne within 24 business hours of payment. Express Post then carries the parcel, and a signature is required. If everything goes smoothly, the notes arrive mid-week, which leaves a day to check the count and weather the stock. If the address is regional, or the signer is hard to reach, order a day or two earlier. The aim is simple: no scene should depend on the last possible delivery.

## Choosing the right delivery address

The best address is one where someone is present during business hours: a production office, a studio, a prop room or a trusted contact. Avoid addresses where nobody will be home, such as a locked location. If the shoot is at a private home, ask the owner to sign or to be available. If you are travelling, send the order ahead to the production base, and carry only what you need on the day.

## Delivery for events, schools and photographers

The same plan works for non-film buyers. A school fair needs the notes before the stall day, and a teacher or office staff member can sign. A photographer working from a studio can ask the studio manager to hold the parcel. An event company can send the notes to the venue contact. Tell the studio your date, give a name and a mobile number, and plan a day of slack.

## What affects delivery time

- Distance from Melbourne. Interstate and regional routes take longer.
- Public holidays and weekends. Express Post follows the Australia Post calendar.
- Payment timing. Dispatch starts once payment is confirmed, so pay early.
- The signature requirement. A missed delivery adds a day or more.
- Address accuracy. A wrong unit number or postcode costs time.

## Tracking and communication

Once the parcel is dispatched, you receive tracking details. Check them each morning in the week of the shoot. If the status looks stuck, contact Australia Post first, then the studio. Keep your phone near you on delivery day, because the courier may call. A small amount of attention at this stage avoids most missed deliveries, and it keeps the cash scene on schedule.

## Returns and exchanges

If a delivery arrives damaged or the count is wrong, tell us the same day with photos of the parcel, the packing and the notes. Keep the original packaging. We will arrange the right fix, whether that is a replacement stack or a correction. Because every order is invoiced and signed for, there is a clear record for both sides.

### Toy Money and Play Money for Kids' Games and Learning
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/toy-money-and-play-money-for-kids-games-and-learning/
- Published: 2026-08-08

Toy money is one of the oldest teaching tools in the classroom and one of the most popular props for children's games. A pile of bright notes turns a lounge room into a shop, a bank or a casino, and it teaches counting, addition, change and the basics of budgeting without any real cash on the table. This guide explains how to choose toy money in Australia, what separates a good pack from a poor one, how to use it for learning and games, how much to buy and what safety and legal points to keep in mind. It is general information, not legal advice. All PROPPS products are non-legal tender props, and our play money packs carry visible markings.

## The short answer

Choose toy money that is clearly not real, durable enough for small hands, easy to count in round denominations and sold in quantities that match the activity. For games and classrooms, bright and simple beats realistic. If you need money that has to look real on camera, you want prop money instead, and our guide to [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) explains the difference.

## What toy money is used for

Teachers, parents, party hosts and community groups use toy money for a wide range of things.

- Maths and money skills. Counting notes, giving change and comparing prices are far easier with something to hold.
- Role-play. Shop, bank, cafe and market games help children practise conversation and negotiation.
- Board and card games. Home-made and commercial games both use notes as a scoring and trading system.
- Classroom economies. Some teachers run a classroom currency to reward effort and teach saving and spending.
- Parties and fundraisers. Casino nights, game stalls and school fairs often use play money in place of real stakes.
- Drama and school productions. A stage cash scene with children usually uses play money, because it is safe and obviously pretend.

## What to look for in toy money

### Clearly not real

Good toy money is designed so nobody could mistake it for genuine currency. Bright colours, simple designs and obvious differences in size are all useful. That is a safety feature as well as a teaching feature: it removes any chance of a child, or an adult, treating the notes as real.

### Durable stock

Notes that tear after one game are frustrating and wasteful. Look for heavier paper or a laminated or coated finish for classroom sets that will be used for years. Rounded corners help younger children.

### Sensible denominations

A set that includes small and large values makes a better teaching tool. Notes of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 let children practise adding and giving change. Avoid sets that are all high values, which make arithmetic harder and games quicker to end.

### Enough notes

A class of thirty children running a market needs far more notes than a family board game. As a rule of thumb, plan on a few dozen notes per child for a shop role-play, and more for a classroom economy that runs over weeks.

## Toy money, play money and pretend money: are they the same?

In everyday use, toy money, play money and pretend money all describe the same thing: notes made for games and learning. Retailers may use one term over another, but the product is the same. What matters is not the label but the features: clearly marked, clearly different from real notes and made to handle.

Our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) include play money packs that carry visible markings and use the same print quality as our film range, so they photograph well at a party and cannot be mistaken for the real thing.

## Teaching with toy money

Here are five activities that work in a classroom or at home.

1. The class shop. Set up a pretend shop with price tags. Children take turns as shopkeeper and customer, practise paying with exact money and then with change.
2. Bank and savings. One child is the bank. Others deposit notes and learn about saving, interest and borrowing in a simple form.
3. Budget challenge. Give each child a fixed amount and a list of items with prices. They plan what to buy.
4. Market day. Children make something, price it and sell it to classmates using toy money, learning supply and demand without any real cost.
5. Round the table. At home, let children handle the weekly pocket money jar with play notes first, then move to real coins once they understand.

Keep the notes in labelled envelopes by value, and make counting them back in part of the lesson. That teaches sorting and responsibility as well.

## Games and parties

For a casino night, a fundraiser or a themed party, toy money does the job and keeps the stakes pretend. Hand out an equal amount to each guest, run the games, and finish with a prize table where the winners swap notes for items. Collect all the notes at the end so none leave the room. For a more polished look for photos, some hosts add a small stack of clearly marked prop notes to the prize table, kept out of circulation. Our guide to [novelty money for parties and events](/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/) explains what is sensible.

## Running a term-long classroom economy

Some teachers run a classroom currency for a whole term. Children earn notes for effort and kindness, pay rent for their desks, save towards a class party and spend at a weekly shop. It works best with a few simple rules: pay on a fixed day each week, keep a class bank that records balances, and set prices so that saving for a week is possible but spending everything is also a real choice. Order enough notes for the whole term in one go, in round denominations, and store them in a labelled box so nothing is lost between lessons. At the end of the term, count what is left, reuse the notes next year and keep a spare set for replacement.

## Teaching tips that make toy money work harder

Start small. Introduce one or two denominations first, then add more as children gain confidence. Let children make mistakes with change and talk through the answer. Mix real prices with pretend ones, so a pencil costs a few dollars and a toy costs a few more. Rotate roles so that every child plays shopkeeper, customer and banker. Finish each session with a short recap of what was learned, and keep a tidy-up routine so counting the notes back in becomes part of the lesson.

## A buying checklist

1. Are the notes clearly not real, with obvious differences in colour and design?
2. Are they durable enough for repeated handling?
3. Do the denominations suit the maths you want to teach?
4. Is the quantity right for the number of children or guests?
5. Do the notes carry visible markings, so anyone who finds one knows what it is?
6. Can you get an invoice for the school or the committee?

## Safety and legal points

Toy money is very low risk. A few simple habits keep it that way.

- Never use toy money as payment. It is not legal tender and a shop assistant is entitled to refuse it.
- Keep it away from the very young. Small notes can be a choking hazard for toddlers, so supervise young children.
- Do not let children carry it out of the house or school. A pocket of play notes in a real shop causes confusion.
- Choose marked notes. Packs with visible markings make the purpose obvious to anyone who finds one.
- Check realism. If a set looks very close to real banknotes, treat it like prop money: keep it controlled and marked. Our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains the law, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

## How much to buy and what it costs

The right quantity depends on the activity. A family game needs a few dozen notes. A classroom shop for twenty-five children needs several hundred. A school fair stall may need more. PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by Australia Post Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD. That minimum suits schools, fundraising committees and event hosts ordering for a whole term or a whole event. For larger runs, ask about wholesale rates on the [wholesale page](/wholesale/).

## Where to go next

Browse [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) for play money, read about [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) if you are unsure which you need, or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your quantity and deadline.

### Prop Money for Content Creators: Social Media & Photoshoot Guidelines
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/
- Published: 2026-07-19

Cash looks great on camera. A fan of notes in a music video, a stack on a desk in a business reel, a scatter on a bed in a fashion shoot: prop money is a staple of content creation. It is also the kind of image that gets shared, screenshotted and misunderstood. A clip that looks like a real giveaway, a real payment or a real stash can attract complaints, platform strikes and uncomfortable questions. This guide is written for content creators, music video directors, social media managers and photographers. It explains how to use prop money for content creators safely, how to present it honestly, how to light and style it, how much to buy and what to avoid. It is general information, not legal advice. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Use marked prop notes, keep them clearly props in the frame or the caption, never present them as real cash, a real giveaway or a real payment, keep them inside the shoot and never spend them. A fan, a stack and a few loose notes cover most content. Buy matte, double-sided notes so they read well on camera.

## Why creators use prop money

Real cash is a poor choice for content. It is risky to carry, hard to insure and impossible to match across a series of shots. It cannot be weathered, thrown or cut. Prop money is consistent, replaceable and safe to handle, and it can be styled to match the brief. For music videos, which often use cash as a visual shorthand for success, and for social media, where a quick cash shot grabs attention, prop notes are the practical option.

## What counts as honest presentation

The risk with cash content is not the notes. It is the message. A few simple rules keep the message honest.

1. Do not suggest the money is real if it is not. A caption such as "I just won" over a stack of prop notes is misleading.
2. Do not run a cash giveaway with prop money. A giveaway promises something real. If you are giving away real money, use real money and follow the platform and legal rules for competitions.
3. Do not pay anyone with prop notes. Not as a joke, not as a test.
4. Do not hand prop notes to strangers on camera. A clip of a stranger accepting a bundle looks like a real gift.
5. Caption it. "Prop money" or "specimen notes" removes doubt.
6. Show the markings sometimes. A close-up of the specimen marking in one frame makes the prop obvious.

## Music videos

Music videos use cash for texture, status and story. A few practical points:

- Plan the money shots. A fan for a close-up, a stack on a table, a bag for a scene that ends in a getaway.
- Choose denominations for colour. $100 and $50 notes read strongly on camera. Our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) helps.
