- Light it softly. Cash under hard light shows glare. Read our guide to [lighting prop money](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/).
- Brief the cast and crew. Dancers, extras and friends in the shot need to know the notes are props and must not be taken home.
- Shoot in controlled places. A studio or a private location is safer than a public street. If you shoot in public, tell the venue and the local police beforehand.
- Count in and out. One person holds the notes and counts them at the end of the day.

## Social media content

Short videos and photos travel fast and lose their context quickly. A clip with prop cash may be shared without the caption. A few extra steps help:

1. Put the context in the video, not only the caption. A line of on-screen text saying "prop money" survives a share.
2. Avoid titles that imply a real payout. A title such as "I gave away $10,000" is a claim, and platforms and regulators may treat it as one.
3. Show the setup. A behind-the-scenes shot with the notes on a prop table makes the context clear.
4. Check platform rules. Some platforms have policies about depicting money, giveaways and scams.
5. Respond to comments. If a viewer asks whether the money is real, say it is a prop.

## Photo shoots

A photo shoot is the easiest place to use prop money well, because it happens in a controlled environment. Use a fan, a stack and a few loose notes. Light them from the side to avoid glare. Keep fingerprints off the surface. Our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/) goes through styling and lighting in detail.

## What to buy

A single creator or small crew needs less than a film set. Plan on:

- One hero set. A fan of notes and a strapped stack.
- A few loose notes. For scatter and continuity.
- A reserve. A sealed stack in case a note is damaged.

PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD. Crypto payments receive a 10% discount. A Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack clears the minimum at $315 and covers most creator needs. Our guide to [how much prop money you need](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) helps you size an order, and the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) shows the options.

## What the law cares about

The Commonwealth Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at counterfeit currency and at reproductions that could deceive a reasonable person. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. Marked prop notes used as props are treated very differently from notes made to pass as real. Never spend prop notes, never offer them as payment and never present them in a way that could mislead. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the standard PROPPS builds to. If you have a concern about counterfeit currency, the [Australian Federal Police](https://www.afp.gov.au/) is the contact.

## Common creator mistakes

- Running a fake giveaway. Not worth the risk.
- Leaving notes in a car or a bag. They end up where they should not.
- Cropping out the markings. Keep them visible in some frames.
- Posting without context. A caption saves trouble.
- Letting friends keep notes. One note in a wallet becomes a question.
- Using play money for a close-up. It looks like a toy. See [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/).

## A creator checklist

1. Marked notes ordered with an invoice.
2. One person in charge of the notes.
3. Cast and crew briefed.
4. Context planned for the caption and the video.
5. Lighting tested.
6. Notes counted in and out.
7. Notes stored safely after the shoot.

## Working with brands and sponsors

If a brand sponsors your content, tell them how the money will be used. Brands care about how a video looks next to their name, and some have rules about showing cash. Agree the caption, the on-screen text and the way the notes are handled before you shoot. A short written note covering "marked prop notes, never spent, never offered as a prize" avoids misunderstandings later.

## Handling comments and questions

Viewers ask whether the money is real. Answer plainly. A pinned comment or a reply that says the notes are specimen-marked props takes the heat out of the thread. If someone suggests the clip is a scam, correct it early and keep a screenshot of the markings and the invoice. A calm, factual reply protects your channel and your sponsors.

## A simple shoot-day routine

1. Count the notes in and photograph them.
2. Brief everyone on set about the notes.
3. Shoot the money shots first, while the notes are fresh.
4. Keep the notes on a tray, not in pockets.
5. Count out at the end and bag them.
6. Store the bag with the shoot kit, not in a bag you carry around town.

## Keeping your channel safe

Platforms respond to complaints quickly. Keep the invoice, a photo of the markings and a note of the shoot date in a folder, so you can answer a query in minutes. Avoid thumbnails that show a stack with a claim of a win. A calm, clear explanation usually settles a dispute.

## Where to go next

See the [photography props range](/shop/photography-props/), the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your brief.

### Prop Cash for Heist and Bank Scenes: Getting the Volume Right
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/
- Published: 2026-07-09

Heist films live and die on the money shot. The vault door opens, the camera pans across rows of bundled cash, and the audience believes the stakes. Getting the volume wrong in either direction hurts: too little and the vault looks half-empty, too much and the budget disappears into bundles the lens never sees. This guide shows how to plan a money stack Australia productions can afford for heist, bank and cash-room scenes. It covers how to count what the camera sees, how to build a vault, how to dress bags, counters and tables, how to use depth and filler, and how to plan quantities, delivery and reuse. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Count shelves, pallets and bags in the frame, work out how many bundles each holds, put hero stacks at the front and let depth and filler handle the rest. A modest vault is about 10 stacks, a larger set with pallets suits 50 Stacks and a full cash room is where 100 Stacks and a wholesale conversation make sense. Order once, keep a reserve and keep notes under the prop master's control.

## What the camera really sees

A vault is mostly shape. The camera sees the front face of each bundle, the colour and the pattern of stacks, not the cash behind. That is why hero stacks at the front matter and the rest can be matching stock or filler. Think of the set as layers.

- Foreground. Hero stacks, held or placed within reach of the actor. These are the notes in close-up.
- Midground. Bundles on shelves, tables and in open bags. Matching stacks keep continuity.
- Background. Depth of field blurs these. Colour and shape matter more than detail.

## Sizing a vault, step by step

1. Measure the set. Count shelves, bays, pallets, cages and open bags.
2. Estimate bundles per unit. How many bundles does a shelf hold? How many does a pallet hold?
3. Multiply. Bundles per unit times units gives total bundles.
4. Convert to stacks. Our stack tiers are Starter, 1, 5, 10, 50 and 100 Stacks. Find the nearest tier.
5. Split by layer. Put hero stock in the foreground and matching stock behind.
6. Add a reserve. One sealed stack is cheap insurance.

For the tiers and prices, see [$100 prop money bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) and [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/).

## Bags, briefcases and counters

### A bag or briefcase

A briefcase opened to the camera shows a thick bundle on top and stacks packed tight. Five stacks usually fill a briefcase to the lip. Put $100 and $50 notes on the visible faces and filler beneath.

### A bank counter

A teller counter needs a handful of hero bundles on the surface and a mix of denominations in the drawer. A Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack often covers a counter and a till. Mix in $20 and $10 notes for the drawer, as the [banknote denominations guide](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) explains.

### A table spread

A table needs volume without depth. One or two stacks, loosely arranged, read as a natural pile. Avoid a perfect grid.

### A duffel or sports bag

A bag unzipped shows the top layer of bundles. Pack a few hero bundles on top and fill the rest with filler. Add a few loose notes at the opening for a lived-in look.

## Depth, filler and tricks

Art departments rarely fill a whole vault with hero notes. These are the usual tricks.

1. Hero faces, cheap cores. Wrap hero notes around filler blocks so the faces read as cash.
2. Repeat stacks. The same stack moved between shots reads as a larger pile on screen.
3. Use depth of field. Blur hides detail.
4. Mix colours. Strapped $100 and $50 bundles together look richer than one colour.
5. Break the order. Spilled notes and a half-open bag add realism.
6. Frame tight. A tight shot needs fewer stacks than a wide.

## Weathering and continuity

A bank vault is clean, a getaway bag is rough. Weather the notes that are handled, leave the vault bundles crisp and keep a log of what went where. Our [art department guide](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/) covers the methods. Photograph the set-up before the first take, and reset to the photo for every take. Count the stacks in and out at the end of each day.

## Lighting a vault

A vault is a hard set to light, because shelves and cages cast shadows and metal throws reflections. Keep light soft, flag the key off the lens axis and test the notes at working distance. Our [lighting guide](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) goes through it. Matte paper helps, because it avoids hot spots.

## Planning quantities, delivery and reuse

Order the full quantity once for a block of shooting. PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD, with a 10% discount for crypto payments. For larger orders, ask about wholesale tiers of 10% to 30% off on the [wholesale page](/wholesale/). After the shoot, keep the stacks for pickups and reshoots, or reuse them in another scene.

## Safety and compliance on a heist set

A heist scene is the kind of scene that attracts attention, especially on location. If you shoot in or near a bank or a shop, tell the venue and the local police beforehand, and keep the supplier invoice on set. Keep notes under the prop master's control, never leave them in a vehicle, and never let background performers keep souvenirs. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [Reserve Bank guidance](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/).

## Planning the shot list around the money

Work with the director to list the money shots. The vault reveal, the bag being filled, the counter exchange and the final spill are all different shots with different needs. Some need volume, some need quality. A pan across shelves needs matching stacks. A close-up on a hand picking up a bundle needs a hero stack. Rank the shots by importance and spend the budget where the camera lingers.

## Fire, water and special effects

If a scene involves fire, water, dust or explosions near the cash, talk to your special effects supervisor early. Paper notes burn, swell and stain, so plan for duplicates and protect the stock you need for other scenes. Do not use real flame near prop notes without the supervisor and the safety plan in place, and keep a separate set of notes for the effect shots, so the hero stock stays clean.

## Crowds, extras and the public

A heist scene shot in public draws attention. Tell the venue and the local police beforehand, brief the extras that the notes are props and keep them under the prop master. Do not hand notes to background performers. If a member of the public asks, show the specimen markings and the invoice. Our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains why the markings matter.

## Wrap and clean-up

At the end of the day count the stacks, bag them, label the bags and lock them away. Collect spilled notes from the floor, the bags and the set. Check pockets, bags and vehicles before the crew leaves. A missing note is a small problem on a set and a bigger one on a street. Log the count and the condition, and store the weathered and clean stock separately.

## Budget notes for a heist sequence

A heist sequence usually has more than one cash moment: the reveal, the handover, the escape and the aftermath. Budget the notes across the whole sequence, not scene by scene, and reuse stacks where the story allows. A single large order with a reserve is almost always cheaper than three small ones, and the stacks will match.

## Reusing stock across a sequence

Stacks that appear in the vault can reappear in the van, the safehouse and the final reveal, provided continuity allows. Photograph each set-up, tag the stacks and keep a movement log, so the same bundles look the same in every scene. Reuse saves money and makes the cash feel like one story rather than several props.

## Budget notes for a heist sequence

A heist sequence usually has more than one cash moment: the reveal, the handover, the escape and the aftermath. Budget the notes across the whole sequence, not scene by scene, and reuse stacks where the story allows. A single large order with a reserve is almost always cheaper than three small ones, and the stacks will match.

## Where to go next

Browse [money stacks](/shop/money-stacks/), the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your vault dimensions and shot list.

### Buying Film Props in Australia: A Checklist for Art Departments
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/buying-film-props-in-australia-a-checklist-for-art-departments/
- Published: 2026-06-19

Buying props for a screen production in Australia is a mix of planning, sourcing and paperwork. Furniture can be hired, costumes can be made, but cash and currency need special care, because the law treats reproductions of banknotes differently from a chair or a lamp. This guide is a buying checklist for art departments, prop masters and line producers. It covers how to brief, where movie props in Australia come from, what to check before you order, how to budget, how to handle delivery and storage and how to keep the paperwork in order, with a focus on currency props. It is general information, not legal advice. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

List every cash scene, count what the camera sees, choose a specialist supplier with marked notes, an ABN and signed-for delivery, order the full quantity once, and file the invoice. For currency, the supplier matters as much as the price, because markings, paper and paperwork are what keep the props lawful and the production protected.

## Step one: write the brief

A clear brief prevents most buying problems. For each cash scene, note:

1. What is shown. A wallet, a till, a briefcase, a vault.
2. How it is handled. Held, counted, thrown, hidden or left on a table.
3. The camera distance. Wide, medium, close-up or insert.
4. The number of takes and set-ups.
5. The look. New, used or aged.
6. The era. Contemporary or period.
7. The date. When the notes must be on set.

Share the brief with the director and the DOP, and keep a copy on the production file.

## Step two: choose where to buy

Movie props Australia wide come from several sources.

- A prop hire house. Good for furniture and general set dressing. Currency stock is usually limited.
- A specialist currency studio. Best for cash scenes that need volume, matching stacks and paperwork. PROPPS is one, based in Eltham, Melbourne, supplying Australian productions since 2019.
- A general prop shop. Useful for small items and last-minute needs.
- Overseas marketplaces. Cheap and fast to find, but with weaker markings, longer delivery and more legal risk. See [local vs overseas suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/).
- Making your own. Not recommended for currency.

You can buy movie props online in Australia for the cash scene from a specialist, and keep the rest of the set dressing with a general supplier. See [film and TV props](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) for our currency packs.

## Step three: check the supplier

Before you order currency props, check:

1. Specimen markings on every note. Ask for a photo of the front and back of a real note.
2. Paper. Genuine Australian banknotes are polymer. Reproductions on paper are easy to tell apart by touch. PROPPS prints on 120gsm matte archival paper.
3. Business details. An ABN, a physical address and a working phone number.
4. Honest descriptions. The listing should say the notes are non-legal tender props.
5. Delivery. Traceable shipping with a signature.
6. Policies. Published shipping, refund and privacy policies.
7. Paperwork. An invoice for the production file.

Our guide to [where to buy prop money in Australia legally](/blog/where-to-buy-prop-money-in-australia-legally/) goes through these in detail.

## Step four: size the order

Count the stacks the camera sees, add the hidden ones, double for repeat set-ups and keep one sealed as a reserve. Our guide to [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) gives examples, and the stack tiers run from a Starter Stack at $115 to 100 Stacks at $14,000. Orders start at $300 AUD.

## Step five: set the budget

A currency budget has four lines.

- Notes. Priced by stack tier and denomination.
- Delivery. Free from $500 AUD at PROPPS.
- Weathering and prep. Art department time and materials.
- Reserve. A sealed stack for late changes.

If the production will need cash across a season, ask about wholesale tiers. See the [wholesale guide](/blog/wholesale-prop-money-for-production-companies-bulk-pricing-explained/) and the [wholesale page](/wholesale/).

## Step six: plan delivery and storage

Express Post needs a signature, so nominate someone at the delivery address. Dispatch leaves our Melbourne studio within 24 business hours of payment. Plan delivery a few days before the first cash scene, not the morning of. On arrival, check the count and the condition, file the invoice and store the notes with the prop master in a secure, dry place. Read [shipping and dispatch](/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/) for timing.

## Step seven: keep the paperwork

A simple production file covers most questions from insurers, location owners and police:

- The supplier's invoice, with the business name, ABN and address.
- A photo of the front and back of a note.
- A line in the call sheet or prop schedule naming the scene and the person responsible.
- A log of notes in and out each day.

Our [compliance page](/compliance/) and [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explain the standard behind the markings.

## Common buying mistakes

- Leaving it until the week of the shoot. Express dispatch is fast, but a late order costs more.
- Choosing on price alone. A cheap listing often means no markings, no invoice and no one to call.
- Forgetting the reserve. A late change forces a rush.
- No storage plan. Notes left in a car or on location are a risk.
- No paperwork. A reshoot or an insurance question needs the file.

## Hire or buy?

Furniture, lamps and large set pieces are usually hired, because the production does not need them after the shoot. Consumables, such as cash, food and anything that will be damaged or weathered, are bought. Currency sits in the second group: weathered notes cannot go back on the shelf, and many productions want a matching reserve for pickups. If the same cash appears across a series, buying once and reusing is usually cheaper than hiring repeatedly.

## Working with a supplier

A good supplier makes the job easier. Send a short brief with the scenes, the quantities, the denominations and the dates. Ask for the invoice and a photo of the notes. Confirm the delivery address and who will sign. Ask about reorder options if the script changes. If you have questions about marking, packaging or timing, ask before you order, not after. A supplier who answers quickly before the sale will answer quickly after it.

## Handling a late change

Scripts change. A table spread becomes a vault, a second day of shooting is added, a reshoot appears. A sealed reserve is the first defence. The second is a supplier who can dispatch fast: PROPPS dispatches within 24 business hours of payment by Australia Post Express. The third is a clear order history, so you can reorder matching stock. Tell the studio what changed and when you need the notes, and we will say what is realistic.

## After the shoot

At wrap, count the notes, bag them and label the box with the scene, the date and the count. Decide whether to keep them for pickups, reuse them on another job or store them with the production records. Do not leave notes loose in a vehicle or a location. Keep the invoice and the log together. If the production ends, store or dispose of the notes sensibly, and never let them out into circulation.

## A one-page buying checklist

1. Brief written and shared.
2. Supplier chosen and checked.
3. Quantity sized from the shots.
4. Reserve included.
5. Budget approved.
6. Delivery date and signer confirmed.
7. Storage plan agreed.
8. Invoice and photo filed.
9. Daily count in place.
10. Wrap plan agreed.

## Questions to ask before you pay

1. Are the notes marked, and can I see a photo?
2. When will the order dispatch, and how will it travel?
3. Who needs to sign for it?
4. Can I reorder matching stock later?
5. Will I get an invoice and a written description for the production file?
6. Is there a price break for a larger or repeat order?

A supplier who answers all six in a few lines is a supplier worth using. If the answers are vague, that is information too. Keep the replies with the production file in case a question comes up after the shoot.

## Lead times and last-minute buys

Good props are rarely last-minute. Allow a few days between order and first use, more if the address is remote or the delivery needs a signature from someone who is on set all day. If you must order late, tell the supplier the date and the delivery address at the start, and ask what is realistic before you pay.

## Questions to ask before you pay

1. Are the notes marked, and can I see a photo?
2. When will the order dispatch, and how will it travel?
3. Who needs to sign for it?
4. Can I reorder matching stock later?
5. Will I get an invoice and a written description for the production file?
6. Is there a price break for a larger or repeat order?

A supplier who answers all six in a few lines is a supplier worth using. If the answers are vague, that is information too. Keep the replies with the production file in case a question comes up after the shoot.

## Where to go next

Browse [film and TV props](/shop/film-and-tv-props/), the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your brief.

### A Brief History of Australian Currency Notes for Set Designers
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/brief-history-of-australian-currency-notes-for-set-designers/
- Published: 2026-05-30

A period drama set in the 1970s does not want a crisp note from last year in the till. A story set in the 1960s may need a different currency altogether. Getting old Australian money notes right on screen takes a little knowledge of the history, because the colours, sizes, designs and even the materials of Australian currency have changed several times. This guide is a short history of Australian banknotes written for set designers, art directors and prop masters. It is not a collectors' catalogue and not a guide to identifying genuine notes. It explains the main eras, what changed and how to dress period cash on screen. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Australia moved from pounds to dollars in 1966, issued paper notes for several decades, introduced polymer banknotes from 1988 and has been updating its designs ever since. For a period set, work out the year of the scene, check what was in circulation and agree the level of accuracy with the director. Many productions choose a plausible look and weathering rather than an exact match, and always keep the notes clearly marked as props.

## Before decimal currency

Before 1966, Australia used pounds, shillings and pence. Notes were issued in pound denominations and were larger and plainer than modern notes. A scene set before the mid-1960s needs a different currency entirely, so the dollar notes in our range are not suitable. For these stories, talk to a specialist prop house and the production's researcher.

## The move to dollars

Decimal currency was introduced in February 1966. The first dollar notes were printed on paper, with a family of colours that made each denomination easy to tell apart. For scenes set from the late 1960s through the 1980s, paper notes with these older looks would have been in the till. These notes are different in size, colour and design from modern notes, so a period set that uses a modern note will look wrong to anyone who remembers the era.

## The polymer era

Australia was an early adopter of polymer banknotes, with the first issued in 1988 for the bicentenary, and a full polymer series followed in the 1990s. Polymer notes last longer, have clear windows and are harder to copy. For scenes set in the 1990s and 2000s, the notes in a wallet would be polymer, with the designs of that series.

## The current series

The Reserve Bank has updated the designs in recent years, introducing new security features and new artwork across the denominations. The current series is what appears in contemporary stories. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes information on its banknotes. Our range covers the five current denominations: $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100. See the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/).

## What this means for set design

1. Decide the year of each scene. A story that jumps between decades may need different cash in each timeline.
2. Work out what is visible. Many scenes show only a corner of a note, which makes accuracy less critical.
3. Match the wear to the era. Old paper notes were soft and often creased. Polymer notes keep their shape longer.
4. Choose accuracy to suit the shot. A close-up on a note needs more care than a background till.
5. Ask for advice. A researcher, a dialogue coach or a prop house with period experience can save a lot of time.

## Dressing period cash with current notes

If a production cannot source period notes, an art department sometimes dresses current-style notes to suggest age. This is a compromise, and it only works when the notes are in the background or the shot is wide. Our notes are matte paper with a soft finish, and they take weathering well. Read our [art department guide to weathering prop cash](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/) for methods. Avoid close-ups of a note that is visibly the wrong era.

## Colours and denominations over time

Denominations have changed along with the designs. The mix of notes that a character would carry in 1975 is not the mix a character would carry today. The $100 note is now associated with large payments, but in earlier decades the largest note in everyday use was lower, and a bundle of the top denomination would look different on screen. When in doubt, ask your researcher what the character would plausibly carry in the year of the scene.

## Period details that matter more than the note

Often the details around the money say more about the era than the note itself. A leather purse, a brown envelope, a pay packet with a name on the front, a cash register with mechanical keys, a coin tray, an old wallet with a worn crease: these are the details the camera picks up. Spend time on them, and the notes will sit comfortably alongside.

## Planning quantities for a period scene

Period scenes often use less cash than modern ones, because people carried smaller sums and used fewer large notes. A pay packet might hold a handful of notes. A shop till might hold a drawer of small denominations. Our guide to [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) explains how to count what the camera sees.

## Compliance

Whatever era you dress, the notes must be clearly marked props. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Never spend them. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [compliance page](/compliance/).

## Delivery and ordering

PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD. Crypto payments receive a 10% discount.

## A short method for researching your era

1. Fix the year. Write the year on the scene breakdown.
2. Find reference photos. Archive photographs, adverts and film stills of the era show cash in use.
3. Check with a researcher. Many productions have one, and local libraries and museums often help.
4. Decide the level of accuracy. A close-up needs more than a wide.
5. Record the decision. Put it on the prop schedule so the next department knows.

## What to ask the director

Ask how visible the money is, whether any shot is an insert on a note, how much the era matters to the story and whether the production will have audiences who know the era well. A period drama broadcast to an audience that lived through the decade will notice a wrong note. A comedy with a quick cut to a till may not. The answers set the budget and the effort.

## Three period examples

A 1970s pay packet. A brown envelope with a name on the front, a handful of notes inside and a few coins. The camera sees the envelope and a corner of paper, so the note itself matters little. Spend the effort on the envelope.

A 1990s shop till. A drawer of mixed notes and coins, with a cash register in view. The register and the receipts carry the era. A few matching notes are enough.

A modern wallet. The camera sees a few notes as a character pays. Use current-series notes, lightly weathered. Our [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) covers this.

## Period mistakes to avoid

- Using a current note in a period close-up. Anyone who remembers the era will notice.
- Over-ageing. Notes in a wallet are soft, not filthy.
- Forgetting the supporting detail. Wallets, envelopes, registers and receipts date a scene more than the money does.
- Ignoring the shot. If the note is out of focus, do not pay for accuracy you cannot see.
- Skipping the paperwork. Even period reproductions must be marked and documented. See our [compliance page](/compliance/).

## Working with the rest of the art department

Cash is only one part of a period look. Talk to the costume department about wallets and purses, to the set decorator about registers and counters and to graphics about receipts and pay packets. Agreeing the details together means the money is never the odd one out in a frame.

## Where to go next

See the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/), browse the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your period and your scene list.

### The Best Australian Banknote Denominations for Film & TV Scenes
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/
- Published: 2026-05-20

Australian banknotes are a visual language. The colours, the sizes and the stacks tell an audience at a glance whether a character is rich or struggling, whether a scene is a legitimate sale or a back-alley deal, and whether the money is a lot or a little. Choosing the right denominations for a scene is one of the quiet decisions an art department makes, and it affects how believable the cash looks. This guide explains the five current Australian denominations, how each reads on camera, which to use for hero stacks, tills and wallets, how to mix them, and how to order the right quantity. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props printed on matte paper, never polymer.

## The short answer

Use $100 and $50 notes for hero stacks and close-ups, because their colours read strongly on camera and signal value at a glance. Use $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills, wallets, tips and everyday purchases, where an all-$100 drawer would look staged. Most scenes use two or three denominations rather than one, and a believable cash scene always mixes them.

## The five current denominations at a glance

The [Reserve Bank of Australia](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) issues five banknotes in the current series, each with its own colour and design. This summary describes how they work on screen, not how to identify genuine notes.

- $5 note. The smallest note, used for tips, coffee, newspapers and small change. Its pinkish-purple tone reads softly and sits naturally in a pocket.
- $10 note. A blue-toned note that suits small purchases, lunches and pocket money.
- $20 note. A red-orange note, the everyday workhorse in wallets, till drawers and ATM scenes.
- $50 note. A gold and yellow note that carries weight on camera and suits bigger purchases, bills and payments.
- $100 note. A green note that signals real money. It is the denomination most associated with bundles, heists and big payments.

Colours vary slightly under different light, so check them on the monitor. Our guide to [lighting prop money on camera](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) explains how to keep them accurate.

## How each denomination reads on camera

### $100 notes

The $100 note is the star of a cash scene. A stack of green reads clearly at a distance and under most lighting. It suits briefcases, tables, vaults and handovers. The risk is overuse: a drawer or wallet of only $100 notes looks like a prop department made it. See the [$100 product](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/), and our guide to [$100 bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/).

### $50 notes

The $50 note's gold reads warmly and gives a stack a rich look. It works well as the top layer of a bundle with lower denominations beneath, and in bills, bribes and payments. See the [$50 product](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/).

### $20 notes

The $20 note is the everyday note. It belongs in wallets, till drawers and ATM scenes. A handful of $20 notes reads as ordinary money, which makes a scene feel real. See the [$20 product](/shop/new-notes/20-australian-prop-money-for-sale/).

### $10 notes

Tens suit small purchases, lunch money and tips. They add variety in a till and a sense of realism in a wallet. See the [$10 product](/shop/new-notes/10-australian-prop-money-for-sale/).

### $5 notes

Fives are for tips, small change and children's pocket money. A few in a wallet or a tip jar completes the picture. See the [$5 product](/shop/new-notes/5-australian-prop-money-for-sale/).

## Mixing denominations by scene

Here are common scenes and a sensible mix.

- A bank counter: strapped bundles of $100 and $50 on the counter, with $20 and $10 notes in the teller's drawer.
- A shop till: a mix of $50, $20, $10 and $5 notes in the tray, with a few $100 notes under the tray.
- A wallet or handbag: two or three $20 notes, a $10 and a $5, with one $50 for variety.
- A briefcase or handover: $100 and $50 on the visible faces, with filler beneath.
- A vault or cash room: $100 stacks in the foreground, with a mix behind.
- A kitchen table or bedroom stash: a loose mix of $50, $20 and $10, creased and unevenly stacked.
- A tip jar or busker's hat: $5, $10 and a few coins.

## Realism tips

1. Match the character. A character who carries $20s is a different person from one who carries $100s.
2. Weather the everyday notes. Small notes are handled more. Our [art department guide](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/) shows how.
3. Use strapped stacks for banks and criminals. Loose notes suggest someone who spends cash daily.
4. Do not match the stack too neatly. Real money is slightly irregular.
5. Keep the same notes for the same story. If money appears before and after a handover, match the stacks.

## Planning quantities

The right quantity depends on what the camera sees. A wallet needs a few notes. A till needs a handful of each denomination. A vault needs stacks. Our [how much prop money guide](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) explains the method, and the stack tiers run from a Starter Stack at $115 to 100 Stacks at $14,000. Orders start at $300 AUD and delivery is free from $500 AUD, with a 10% discount for crypto payments.

## Period and international notes

Productions set in earlier decades sometimes need older note designs, which have different colours and sizes. If your story is set in the past, tell the art department early, and read our [history of Australian currency notes for set designers](/blog/brief-history-of-australian-currency-notes-for-set-designers/). Productions shooting overseas stories may need other currencies, which PROPPS does not currently supply. We make Australian dollar props only.

## Compliance

Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on matte paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Never spend them, and keep them under the prop master's control. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the full standard.

## Reading a denomination mix from the script

Start with the character. A student with a part-time job carries a few $20 notes and some coins. A tradesperson paid in cash carries a roll of $50s and $20s. A bank manager has crisp, strapped bundles. A small-time crook has a mix of everything, crumpled and folded. A retail worker has a till of small notes and a bag of coins. When the script says "he pays", ask what he is paying for. A coffee is a $5 or a $10. A used car is a bundle of $100s. The denomination is part of the story.

## Denominations and the size of the sum

Audiences judge the size of a sum by the size of the stack and the colour on top. A thin stack of $100s reads as a few thousand dollars. A thick stack of $20s reads as the same sum but looks a little desperate. If a scene needs to feel like a lot of money in a small space, use $100s. If it needs to feel like money scraped together, use $20s and $10s. Our [$100 bundle size guide](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) shows how many stacks the camera needs.

## Mixing mistakes to avoid

- All one denomination. A till or a wallet of only $100 notes looks staged.
- Too many large notes in everyday scenes. A shop till rarely holds many $100s.
- Uniform wear. Real notes in the same wallet have different ages.
- Ignoring colour in the grade. If the grade desaturates greens, a $100 stack may lose its punch. Check the notes in the grade, not only on set.
- Forgetting continuity. If a character pays with a $50 and receives change, the notes on screen should add up.

## Ordering by denomination

Each denomination is a separate product in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), and the stack tiers are the same across all five. For a typical drama, order the hero denominations in the larger tiers and the small ones in a Starter Stack. A single order combining several denominations also helps reach the $300 minimum and the $500 free delivery threshold. If you are unsure about the mix, send the scene list through the [contact page](/contact/) and we will suggest one.

## Small details that sell the cash

Rubber bands, paper clips and folded receipts make a bundle look like it belongs to a person. A $5 note folded in half in a back pocket tells a different story from the same note flat in a wallet. Think about how the money is carried, not just what it is.

## Where to go next

Browse the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), compare the individual denominations above or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your scene list.

### Fake Money vs Prop Money: Understanding the Legal Difference in Australia
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/fake-money-vs-prop-money-the-legal-difference-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-05-10

Search for "fake money" in Australia and you will find everything from board game tokens to listings that cross a legal line. The phrase covers too much ground to be useful, and the difference between lawful imitation money for a production and an offence under Commonwealth law is not a matter of taste. This guide explains the vocabulary, the tests that separate prop money from counterfeit currency, and the questions to ask before you buy. It is general information, not legal advice.

## Why the words matter

People use "fake money", "imitation money", "play money", "toy money", "prop money", "replica notes" and "counterfeit" as if they were interchangeable. They are not, and a supplier who uses them loosely is telling you something about how careful they are.

- Play money and toy money are obviously not real. They are brightly coloured, different in size and designed for games, classrooms and children. They carry almost no legal risk.
- Prop money is reproduction currency made for motion pictures, television, theatre, photography and training. It is designed to look right on camera while remaining clearly marked and clearly different in the hand.
- Imitation money is the broad everyday term for any of the above. On its own it tells you nothing about legality.
- Counterfeit currency is made or used to deceive. It is a criminal matter, and nothing in this article describes how to make it or where to get it.

## The legal line in one paragraph

The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) protects Australian currency. The law cares about whether an item could deceive a reasonable person into accepting it as genuine, and about what someone does with it. A reproduction with clear, permanent specimen markings, a different material and size or treatment, and honest marketing sits on the lawful side. A note made to pass at a till does not. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains how PROPPS builds to Section 22 and the Reserve Bank's reproduction guidance.

## Four tests that separate prop money from counterfeit

Use these four tests on any supplier, including us.

### 1. Is it marked?

Every note should carry permanent, prominent markings such as SPECIMEN or a statement that it is for motion picture use only. Markings that can be rubbed off, cropped out or hidden in fine print do not count. Ask for a photo of the note's front and back before you order.

### 2. Is it different from a genuine note?

Real Australian banknotes are printed on polymer and carry layered security features. A prop that is also polymer and copies every feature is not a prop in any sense that matters. PROPPS prints on non-reflective archival paper, which reads correctly on camera and feels different in the hand.

### 3. Is the marketing honest?

A legitimate seller describes the product as a prop, names the permitted uses and states that it is not legal tender. Warning signs include phrases about passing detection tests, "undetectable" quality, unmarked or discreet delivery, and unsourced claims of government clearance. Honest copy never suggests you can spend the product.

### 4. Is the intended use legitimate?

Film, television, theatre, advertising, photography, art and simulation training are all clear uses. A "prank" at a restaurant, a social media stunt that presents prop cash as real, or any attempt to pay for something is misuse, whatever the notes were bought for.

## Comparing the options

Here is how the common categories line up for a buyer:

- Board game and toy money: safe, but looks wrong on camera and is not made for production use. Our guide to [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) covers the choice.
- Marked prop currency from a local studio: the right choice for a scene that needs realism and a paper trail.
- Unmarked "realistic" notes from marketplace sellers: the highest risk. They may be held at the border, and a buyer who cannot show specimen markings has nothing to show a police officer or an insurer.
- Anything described as counterfeit or sold to be spent: illegal. Do not buy it.

## What this looks like on a real production

A drama set in a bank needs a few hundred $100 notes in the drawer and one hero stack on the counter. The art department orders marked notes from an Australian supplier, files the invoice, stores the notes with the prop master and counts them in and out each shooting day. When a location owner asks what the cash is, the answer is a one-page supplier statement and a note in the call sheet.

A photographer shooting a lifestyle campaign uses a fanned handful of $50 notes. The notes are marked, the shoot is in a studio, and nothing leaves the building. Compare that with a content creator who films themselves handing prop cash to strangers: the notes are identical, but the use is not.

Read more on the creator side in our [guide to prop money for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) and our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).

## Questions to ask before you buy

1. Are the notes marked, and can I see a photo of the markings?
2. Is the supplier an Australian business with an ABN and a physical address?
3. What material are the notes printed on?
4. How are they delivered, and is a signature required?
5. Does the seller state what the notes may and may not be used for?
6. Will I get an invoice and a written description I can put on the production file?

## Common myths

"If it is clearly a prop, nothing can go wrong." The markings protect you only when they are on the note and you can show them. A prop kept in a wallet, spent or posted as real cash loses the protection that the markings and the invoice give you.

"A disclaimer in the listing is enough." A line of small print on a website does not travel with the note. The marking has to be on the note itself, where anyone who picks it up can read it.

"Overseas notes are the same, only cheaper." They often are not. Polymer notes that copy current Australian designs closely are the category most likely to be stopped at the border, and you will have no local supplier to call if something goes wrong.

"Everyone knows it is a prop on a film set." The crew do. A bank teller, a shopkeeper or a passer-by watching a street shoot does not. Briefing the venue first is part of using prop money responsibly.

"Only big productions need to worry." The rules do not scale with budget. A student short and a feature film both need marked notes, a supplier invoice and a sensible plan for who holds the cash. Smaller crews often have less legal back-up, so a clean paper trail matters more, not less.

## Why we avoid the word "fake" on our product pages

Buyers do search for "fake money", and our guides use that phrase where it helps people find accurate information. But we do not describe products as fake, spendable or lookalike cash, because it frames the product as something it is not. Our notes are reproduction props. They are specimen-marked, they are paper rather than polymer, and they are made for the screen, the stage and the classroom.

## Where to go next

Browse the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), read the guide on [whether it is illegal to buy prop money](/blog/is-it-illegal-to-buy-prop-money-australia/), or see the full [Section 22 explainer](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/). Orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500, and every parcel ships Australia Post Express with signature on delivery.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Check the current legislation and the RBA's guidance, and ask your own lawyer about a specific production.

### Wholesale Prop Money for Production Companies: Bulk Pricing Explained
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/wholesale-prop-money-for-production-companies-bulk-pricing-explained/
- Published: 2026-04-30

Production companies rarely buy prop money once. A series has multiple episodes, a feature has several cash scenes, and a studio may run more than one project at a time. Buying prop cash per scene usually costs more once shipping, handling and mismatched stacks are counted, and it gives the art department a continuity problem. This guide explains the prop money price structure at PROPPS, how bulk and wholesale pricing works, how to plan a season-long order, how to compare quotes fairly and what to ask a supplier. It is written for line producers, production managers, prop masters and accountants. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

The prop money price at PROPPS starts with stack tiers, from $115 for a Starter Stack to $14,000 for 100 Stacks, with orders from $300 AUD and free delivery from $500 AUD. Larger and repeat runs qualify for wholesale tiers of 10% to 30% off, and crypto payments receive a 10% discount. Order the full quantity for a block of shooting to keep stacks matching and keep paperwork simple.

## The standard price tiers

Every product in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) is sold in the same tiers. Sizes are described by face value, and prices are in AUD.

- Starter Stack: $1,500 face value, $115
- 1 Stack: $2,000 face value, $200
- 5 Stacks: $10,000 face value, $850
- 10 Stacks: $20,000 face value, $1,600
- 50 Stacks: $100,000 face value, $7,500
- 100 Stacks: $200,000 face value, $14,000

The price per dollar of face value falls as the tier rises, so one large order costs less than several small ones. Orders start at $300 AUD, and delivery is free from $500 AUD.

## What wholesale adds

Wholesale pricing is for production companies and agencies that order in volume or repeatedly. It typically offers:

- Tiered discounts. Larger runs qualify for 10% to 30% off the standard price.
- A named contact. Reorders do not need to go through the standard checkout each time.
- Matching stock. Stacks from the same run match from episode to episode.
- Planned dispatch. Deliveries can be scheduled around shooting blocks.
- One invoice. A single invoice or a clear schedule simplifies production accounting.

Our [wholesale page](/wholesale/) has the form, and our [money stacks range](/shop/money-stacks/) shows the sizes.

## Why buying per scene costs more

Buying cash one scene at a time looks cheap, but the costs add up.

1. Repeated minimum orders. Each order has a minimum, so several small orders pay it several times.
2. Shipping and signatures. Each delivery needs someone at the address to sign.
3. Mismatched stacks. Notes from different runs can differ slightly in colour and finish.
4. Rush fees. A late scene change forces an urgent order.
5. Admin time. Each order is a purchase order, an invoice and a reconciliation.

Ordering once for a block of shooting removes most of these. It also lets the art department weather and plan the cash as a single set, as our [art department guide](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/) explains.

## Questions your accountant will ask

Production accountants usually want to know the total cost, when it is due, what is included and what the paperwork looks like. Prepare answers: the price per tier, the minimum order and the free delivery threshold, the payment methods, the tax treatment on the invoice and the delivery schedule. A clear quote makes budgeting and cashflow easier, and an invoice that names the notes as specimen-marked props makes the file complete.

## Scheduling deliveries across a shoot block

A single order can still be delivered in stages. Tell the studio when each scene is shot and which stacks are needed first. Dispatch leaves our Melbourne studio within 24 business hours of payment, and Australia Post Express delivery needs a signature, so nominate someone at each address. If a second location is interstate, plan a day for travel. A short schedule sent with the order avoids a missed delivery.

## Storage and security for larger orders

A pallet of stacks is a valuable item for a production, even though the notes are props. Store it in a locked room or cage, give one person the key and keep a movement log. Count in and out each day. Do not leave stacks in vehicles or on location overnight. Treat the notes as production property, because losing a stack mid-shoot costs time even when it costs little money.

## Planning a season order

Use this method to size a wholesale order.

1. List every scene with cash across the season. Use the scripts or the breakdown.
2. Count the visible stacks per scene. Our guide to [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) explains how.
3. Identify reusable stacks. Stacks that appear in several scenes can be bought once.
4. Group by denomination. $100 and $50 hero stacks, plus smaller denominations for tills.
5. Add a reserve of 10% to 15%. Damage, loss and reshoots happen.
6. Round to the nearest tier. Compare the price of two tiers, because a bigger tier can be cheaper than the sum of small ones.

## Comparing quotes fairly

Not every quote is comparable. Ask each supplier the same questions.

- Are the notes specimen-marked on every note? Ask for a photo.
- What is the paper and the weight? PROPPS uses 120gsm matte archival paper.
- Is print double-sided and consistent across runs?
- Are stacks counted and strapped?
- Is delivery traceable with a signature? PROPPS uses Australia Post Express with signature.
- Is there an invoice and paperwork for the production file?
- What is the lead time and the reorder process?

Our guides to [cheap prop money](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) and [local vs overseas suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/) explain why the cheapest quote is not always the lowest cost.

## Payment and paperwork

Wholesale buyers usually need clear paperwork. PROPPS provides an invoice for each order, accepts bank transfer, PayID and crypto, and gives a 10% discount on crypto payments. Keep the invoice on the production file together with a note of the specimen markings. That answers most questions from insurers, location owners and legal teams. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) and [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) set out the standard.

## A worked example

A six-episode series has a bank scene in episode one, a briefcase handover in episode three and a vault scene in episode six, plus recurring tills and wallets in every episode. The line producer plans 5 Stacks for the bank and briefcase scenes, which are reused, 10 Stacks for the vault, and a Starter Stack and 1 Stack per episode for tills and wallets, with a reserve. At standard prices, that comes to roughly $850 plus $1,600 plus six Starter Stacks and six 1 Stacks, before any wholesale discount. Ordering the whole quantity once keeps every stack matched, and the wholesale tier lowers the total further. Tell the studio your breakdown and we will quote.

## Reading a quote line by line

A wholesale quote should show the quantity, the tier, the price, the delivery cost, the payment terms and the estimated dispatch date. If any of these is missing, ask. Check that the quantity matches your plan, that the finish is the one you tested and that the tax treatment is shown. Keep the quote with the production file, because it records what was promised if a problem comes up later.

## Wholesale for agencies and events

Wholesale is not only for film. Agencies buying branded or themed prop notes for several clients, event companies stocking casino-night kits and schools ordering for a whole year can all use the same approach: plan the whole quantity, order once and keep the stock together. Ask about tiers when you send your enquiry, and mention if the order will repeat, because repeat business is part of what wholesale pricing rewards.

## Reordering mid-season

If the script changes or a reshoot is added, reorder from the same run where possible so the new stacks match the old ones. Tell the studio the original order reference and the quantity, and ask about timing. Keep a small reserve from the start, because it is the cheapest insurance against a late change.

## Compliance and handling

Every note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. On a larger order, assign one person to hold the stock, count it in and out each day and keep it in a secure place. Never spend the notes. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

## Where to go next

Send your breakdown through the [wholesale page](/wholesale/), see [money stacks](/shop/money-stacks/) for counted bundles or [contact the studio](/contact/) and we will quote your season.

### Custom & Branded Prop Currency: A Guide for Agencies and Brand Campaigns
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/custom-and-branded-prop-currency-guide-for-agencies/
- Published: 2026-04-20

Branded currency is an old and effective marketing idea. A note with a logo, a mascot or a campaign slogan is memorable, shareable and fun to hand out. Agencies use it for product launches, conference giveaways, loyalty promotions and television segments. The difficulty is that real currency is protected by law, so custom prop money printing in Australia has to be done carefully. This guide is written for agencies, brand teams and event producers. It covers what custom prop money is, how a brief works, how to prepare artwork, what compliance markings are required, how to plan quantities and timing and what to avoid. It is general information, not legal advice. All PROPPS custom runs are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Custom prop money is lawful when it carries permanent specimen markings, differs clearly from genuine currency and is used as a prop or promotional item, never as payment. Give the studio a clear brief, the artwork and the quantity, allow time for proofs and plan how the notes will be distributed. Never ask for a design that copies a real note closely.

## What custom prop money is

Custom prop money, also called branded currency, branded prop notes or custom play money, is printed with your artwork instead of a standard design. Typical examples include:

- Branded launch notes. A product launch where each guest receives a note carrying the product name and a QR code.
- Conference currency. Notes used as tokens at a stand or as prizes in a game.
- Loyalty and promotion notes. A retail campaign where customers collect notes for discounts.
- Television and stage props. A game show or a sketch needing bespoke cash with a fictional bank or character.
- Custom play money. Playful notes with an event or school logo for fairs and fundraisers.

## What the law cares about

The Commonwealth Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at counterfeit currency and at reproductions that could deceive a reasonable person. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. Branded notes that are clearly different from genuine currency, clearly marked and used as promotional props sit on the right side of the line. Notes that closely copy a real note and could be passed off as one do not. Our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains how PROPPS builds to the standard, and you should check the current legislation and speak to a lawyer for anything unusual.

## How a custom brief works

A good brief saves time and money. It usually includes:

1. The purpose. Why are the notes needed, and how will they be used?
2. The audience. Who will receive them, and where?
3. The artwork. Logos, characters, colours, slogans and any QR codes or URLs.
4. The format. Size, denominations or values, and whether the notes are single or double-sided.
5. The quantity. How many of each design.
6. The deadline. The launch date or event date, with a buffer.
7. The budget. An approximate range, so the studio can suggest options.

Tell the studio your concept through the [contact page](/contact/) or on WhatsApp. We reply with a quote and next steps.

## Preparing artwork

Good artwork makes a good note.

- Supply vector files where possible. Logos should be crisp at any size.
- Keep important content away from the edges. Trimming varies slightly.
- Use readable type. A note is small, so avoid fine print for the key message.
- Leave room for the markings. Specimen markings are part of the design, so do not crowd them out.
- Avoid copying real note designs. Use your own illustration, colour scheme and layout. A custom note should look like your brand, not like a bank.
- Think about both sides. The back is a chance for a call to action or a code.

## Compliance markings

Every custom run is held to the same specimen standard as our standard range. That means permanent, prominent markings on every note, paper stock rather than polymer and a clear statement that the notes are not legal tender. These markings are not optional and they are not negotiable, because they are what keeps a custom run lawful. We do not remove or reduce them for a design, and we do not print notes that are intended to pass as real currency.

## Quantities, timing and cost

Quantity drives cost and lead time. Small runs for a launch or a television segment are quicker. Larger runs for a national campaign need more planning. As a rule of thumb:

- Plan for proofs. Allow time for at least one round of changes.
- Add a buffer. Event dates are fixed, and printing and delivery add days.
- Order a spare box. Notes get lost, damaged or taken.
- Ask about wholesale tiers. Larger runs may qualify for better pricing. See the [wholesale page](/wholesale/) and our [wholesale guide](/blog/wholesale-prop-money-for-production-companies-bulk-pricing-explained/).

Standard PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD and ship by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with signature on delivery. Custom runs are quoted per job.

## Campaign ideas that work

Branded notes work best when the idea is simple. A launch where each guest gets a note with a unique code to redeem. A pop-up where notes buy small items at a stand. A loyalty scheme where collecting a set earns a reward. A television segment where contestants play for branded cash. A retail promotion where a note acts as a voucher. In each case, the note supports the story, rather than being the story. Keep the message short, the branding bold and the markings visible.

## Proofs and approvals

Plan for at least one proof. The studio prepares a layout showing the artwork, the markings and the trim. Check spelling, logos, colours and any codes. Ask who needs to approve it, from the brand manager to legal, and get sign-off in writing. Changes after printing are costly, so use the proof stage to catch problems. If a code or URL is on the note, test it before the run.

## Custom or standard: which suits the job?

Standard notes suit film, television, theatre and photography, where the money has to look like real cash on camera. Custom notes suit promotions and events, where the point is to carry a brand. If a scene needs realistic cash, choose standard notes from the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/). If a campaign needs something people keep and share, choose custom. Many projects use both.

## Distributing branded notes

How you hand out the notes matters as much as how they are printed.

1. Give them context. A card or a sign that says what the notes are removes confusion.
2. Do not hand them out near shops or taxi ranks. A note in a pocket can end up at a till.
3. Brief staff. Event staff should know the notes are promotional props.
4. Make them clearly branded. A note with your logo is hard to mistake for real currency.
5. Keep a count. Know how many were printed and how many were given out.

## Social media and PR

Branded notes are made to be photographed. When you share images, make it obvious that the notes are promotional props. A caption such as "our launch notes" is enough. Avoid images that suggest a real cash giveaway unless it really is one and you are following the relevant rules. Our [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) explains how to present prop money honestly.

## Working with an agency timeline

A typical custom job runs in four stages: brief and quote, artwork and proof, print and finish, then dispatch. Build a week of slack into each stage if the date is fixed, and tell the studio the event date at the start. If your client is slow to approve, say so early. A realistic timeline protects the launch, because a late note is worth nothing at the party. Keep one point of contact on each side, and keep all approvals in one email thread.

## What to put in the quote request

To get an accurate quote quickly, include the quantity, the number of designs, the format, any special finish, the delivery address and the date. Attach artwork if you have it, or a description if you do not. Mention whether the notes will be handed out in public or used on camera, because that affects how the markings are placed. The more detail you give, the fewer questions we need to ask.

## Common mistakes

- Copying a real note. It is both a legal risk and a poor brand idea.
- Leaving too little time. Printing, proofs and delivery all take days.
- Forgetting the back. A blank back is a missed chance.
- Skipping the briefing. Event staff and guests need to know what the notes are.
- Printing without a spare. Notes disappear.

## Where to go next

See [custom and branded props](/shop/custom-and-branded-props/) for the range, read the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the standard, or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your brief.

### Novelty Money for Parties and Events: What's Legal in Australia
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-04-10

A stack of cash on a party table, a "money rain" at a themed event, a casino night with a prize wall of notes: novelty money makes events more fun and more photogenic. It also raises the question hosts rarely think about until a guest asks: is this legal? This guide covers novelty prop money in Australia for parties and events. It explains what is generally fine, where the risks are, how to choose between play money and marked prop notes, how to run an event so the notes stay controlled, and what to do afterwards. It is general information, not legal advice. All PROPPS products are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Novelty money is fine at an event when it is clearly marked or obviously not real, when it is used only as a prop and when it stays inside the event. Problems come from realistic unmarked notes, from guests taking them away, from using them as payment and from posting images that suggest the cash is real. Marked notes and a simple control plan solve almost all of it.

## What counts as novelty money

Novelty money covers a wide range.

- Play money and toy money. Obviously not real and the safest choice. See [toy money and play money for kids](/blog/toy-money-and-play-money-for-kids-games-and-learning/).
- Marked prop notes. Realistic enough to look good in photos, with permanent specimen markings and printed on paper. See the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/).
- Custom branded notes. Notes with a brand or event name on them. See [custom and branded props](/shop/custom-and-branded-props/).
- Money guns, confetti cannons and cash-themed decorations. These use notes in a throwaway way and need extra care, because notes end up in the crowd.

## Where the law comes in

The Commonwealth Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at counterfeit currency and reproductions that could deceive a reasonable person. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. In broad terms, notes that are clearly marked and clearly different from genuine currency, and that are used as props, are treated very differently from notes made to pass as real. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) for how PROPPS builds to the standard, and check the current legislation for anything specific to your event.

## Play money or marked prop notes?

Choose by the job.

- A game or fundraiser where guests handle the money: play money. It is cheap, obviously pretend and safe if a note leaves the room.
- A photo wall, a prize table or a themed backdrop: marked prop notes, kept in one place and counted at the end.
- A brand activation with giveaways: custom play money, clearly marked and clearly different from real notes.
- A proposal or a surprise: marked prop notes in a stack or a box, kept with the host.

Our guide to [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) goes into more detail.

## An event control plan

A simple plan keeps novelty money from causing trouble.

1. Choose one person to hold the stock. They count the notes in at the start and out at the end.
2. Hand out only what is needed. Give guests a fixed amount of play money, not a bowl to help themselves from.
3. Brief the staff. Bar staff, door staff and caterers should know the notes are props and must not be accepted as payment.
4. Mark the area. A sign at the casino table or prize wall saying "prop money, not legal tender" removes doubt.
5. Collect at the end. Count, bag and store the notes. Do not let guests take marked prop notes home as souvenirs.
6. Keep the invoice. If the venue or the insurer asks, you can show what the notes are.

## Money rain and cash cannons

Cash cannons, confetti guns and "money rain" effects are popular for stage reveals and dance floors. They are also where novelty money most often leaves the venue. If you use them, use clearly pretend play notes, not realistic prop notes, because the notes will end up in pockets and bags. Sweep the floor, count what you can, and warn the crowd that the notes are novelty. Realistic prop notes are a poor choice for anything that scatters.

## Social media and photography

Photos of cash get shared widely. A picture of a person holding a fan of realistic notes with a caption suggesting a win, a gift or a payment is the kind of post that causes complaints. If you are photographing an event, make it obvious the money is a prop: a sign in the shot, a caption that says so, or notes that are clearly play money. Our [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) explains how to present prop money honestly.

## Planning quantities

The right quantity depends on the activity.

- Casino night: a starting stack per guest, plus extra for the bank.
- Game stall: enough to cover prizes and change for the expected crowd.
- Photo wall or prize table: a few stacks or a handful of fanned notes, not a vault.
- Proposal or reveal: one hero stack or box.

PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by Australia Post Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD. For larger events and school or charity runs, see the [wholesale page](/wholesale/). Our guide to [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) also helps you size a stack.

## Five quick event plans

Birthday casino night. Give each guest the same starting stack of play money, run three or four table games, and finish with a prize table. Count all the notes back in before guests leave.

School or club fundraiser. Sell tickets for play money, run game stalls and let children spend at a prize table. A volunteer holds the cash box and counts notes in and out.

Corporate themed night. Use custom play money with the company name, clearly marked, for team games. Collect it at the end and use it as a prize draw.

Photo wall or backdrop. A few fanned marked prop notes and one stack make a good photo prop. Keep them on the wall, not on the guests.

Proposal or reveal. One stack or box of marked prop notes, held by the host and returned to storage afterwards.

## Choosing a theme and keeping it fun

A good theme makes the money part of the fun rather than the point of it. A roaring twenties night suits stacks of notes and a prize wall. A pirate party suits treasure chests and gold-coloured play money. A school fair suits simple tickets and small notes. Whichever theme you pick, keep the rules simple, hand out equal amounts, and make sure the prizes are worth more than the effort of counting.

## Questions venues and insurers ask

Venues and insurers usually ask three things: what is the money, who is responsible for it and will it leave the building. Be ready with the answers. The money is novelty play money or marked prop notes, one named person looks after it, and it is counted in and out. Having the supplier invoice and a one-line description of the plan on hand answers most questions in seconds.

## After the event

Count the notes back in, store them dry and flat and keep them in a labelled box. Marked notes can be reused for the next event. If you do not need them, keep them with the paperwork rather than throwing them loose in the bin or giving them to guests. Play money can be reused in classrooms and games.

## Common mistakes

- Using realistic notes in a scattering effect. They will leave the venue.
- Letting guests keep marked notes. One note in a wallet can turn into a question later.
- Skipping the briefing. Bar and door staff need to know the notes are props.
- Using notes as payment, even as a joke. Never.
- Removing the markings for a better photo. Do not cut, crop or cover them.

## Where to go next

Browse [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/), see marked notes in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your event details.

### Prop Money for Photography: Getting Realistic Cash Shots Without the Risk
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/
- Published: 2026-03-31

Cash is a powerful visual in photography. A fanned handful of notes says success, a stack on a desk says business, a scatter on a bed says excess. For editorial, product and advertising shoots, photoshoot props Australia wide often include prop money, because real cash is risky to carry, expensive to tie up and easy to damage. This guide is written for photographers, stylists, producers and creative directors. It covers how to choose prop money for a photoshoot, how to light and style it, how to avoid glare and clutter, how to stay on the right side of the law and what to order. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Choose matte, double-sided, specimen-marked notes. Style them in simple, deliberate groups: a fan, a stack and a few loose notes. Light them softly from the side to avoid glare. Keep the notes clearly props in the shot and in the caption, and keep them in the studio. A single set of fanned notes plus one strapped stack covers most set-ups.

## Why photographers use prop money

Real cash is a poor studio prop. It is attached to a risk, because someone must hold it, insure it and count it. It is hard to match across a series of shots, because notes vary in age and wear. It cannot be weathered, marked or cut for a creative idea. Prop money solves all of this. It is consistent, replaceable and safe to handle, and it can be styled to match a brief.

For photography the print has to hold up in high resolution. A camera at a modern resolution will show fine line work and paper grain, so poor print quality is visible in a way it never is on a phone. That is why our [guide to high quality prop money](/blog/high-quality-prop-money-how-to-judge-it-on-camera/) is useful before you order.

## What to look for in prop money for photography

- Matte, non-reflective paper. Glossy stock throws hot spots under strobes and continuous light. PROPPS prints on 120gsm matte archival paper.
- Crisp print at close range. Fine line work should stay clean at the working distance for your lens.
- Double-sided print. A flipped or fanned note shows its back.
- Consistent colour across the order. Notes from different runs can differ slightly, which shows in a flat lay.
- Specimen markings. Every note should carry permanent markings. Ask for a photo of the front and back before you order.
- Denominations that suit the brief. $100 and $50 notes read strongly, while smaller denominations suit a lifestyle or retail story. Our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) helps you choose.

## Styling cash for the camera

### The fan

A fan of notes is the classic cash shot. Hold the notes by one end and spread them in a gentle arc. Keep the spread even, and avoid fanning too many notes or the edges lose definition. Eight to twelve notes make a clean fan.

### The stack

A strapped stack reads as money at a glance. Square the edges, keep the strap flat and let the top note show. A stack on its side shows the layered edges, which is often more convincing than a flat top view.

### The scatter

A scatter of loose notes suggests abundance or chaos. Drop the notes from a short height and let them fall, then adjust a few by hand. Avoid a perfect pattern. Photograph in bursts, because the best scatter is rarely the first.

### The flat lay

A flat lay on a table or a coloured surface needs careful alignment. Use a ruler or a grid on the table, keep the notes parallel, and watch the shadows between them. Soft overhead light from a large source keeps shadows gentle.

### The hand shot

A model holding or counting notes needs a clean, uncreased hero note and a few working notes. Keep fingerprints off the surface and replace hero notes between sets.

## Lighting prop money

Light for the notes the way you light skin: large, soft and angled.
