Place the key at roughly 45 degrees to the table, away from the lens axis, use a flag or a dark card for negative fill and watch the highlights on the paper. Our guide to [lighting prop money on camera without glare](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) goes through this in detail. If you shoot tethered, check a note at 100 percent on the screen, because glare and print softness show up there first.

## Props that pair well with cash

Cash works best with a small number of well-chosen companions. A leather wallet, a briefcase, a watch, a pair of sunglasses, a sleek phone, a paper bag, a champagne glass and a pile of receipts all suggest a story. Keep the palette simple. A neutral background lets the green and gold of the notes carry the image, while a bright background competes with them.

## Working with a stylist and creative director

Agree the look before the shoot day. Share a mood board that shows how the cash should appear: crisp and new, creased and used, or scattered and chaotic. Decide who handles the notes, because a stylist who arranges stacks all day will want clean gloves and a tray. Agree the denominations, the quantity and the number of hero shots, so nobody is surprised by a request for a second vault on the day. A short call before the shoot saves time on set.

## Retouching and post-production

Retouching cash is easier when the capture is clean. Fix stray dust, fingerprints and creases in post, but do not remove or alter the specimen markings on the notes, and do not edit a note to look more like a real banknote. If an image will be used in advertising, keep a copy of the supplier invoice and the order description with the job file, so the client can show what the notes are if anyone asks.

## Keeping the shoot on the right side of the law

Photographs of cash get shared widely, so presentation matters. A few habits protect the client and the photographer.

1. Use marked notes. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings and is printed on paper rather than polymer.
2. Keep the markings visible in at least some frames, or caption the image. A line such as "prop money" removes ambiguity.
3. Do not photograph notes in a way that suggests a real payment or a giveaway. A shot of a hand passing notes to the camera with a caption about a prize is the kind of image that attracts complaints.
4. Keep the notes in the studio. Count them in and out.
5. Never spend them. Not as a test, not as a joke.

Our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains the law behind these habits, and the [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions. For creators posting on social media, read the [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/).

## What to order for a photoshoot

The right order depends on the brief.

- A single hero image: one set of fanned notes and one strapped stack.
- A campaign with several set-ups: two or three stacks of the same denomination, so every image matches, plus a few loose notes.
- A lifestyle series with tills, wallets and counters: a Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack, with a mix of denominations.
- A big visual, such as a bed of cash or a vault: 5 or 10 Stacks, with hero stacks on top.

PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD. Crypto payments receive a 10% discount. Browse the [photography props](/shop/photography-props/) range, or read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) to size an order.

## A pre-shoot checklist

1. Confirm the denominations and quantity with the creative director.
2. Order early enough to allow for a signature on delivery.
3. Test a note under your lights and at your lens distance.
4. Pack gloves, a lint roller and a spare stack.
5. Count the notes in at the start of the day and out at the end.
6. Caption the final images so the notes read as props.

## Where to go next

See the [photography props range](/shop/photography-props/), the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your brief and we will help you choose.

### How Much Prop Money Do You Need for a Scene? A Quantity Guide for Producers
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/
- Published: 2026-03-21

Ordering too little prop money leaves a scene looking thin. Ordering too much puts budget into bundles the lens never sees. The answer is not a single number. It depends on what the camera shows, how many takes and set-ups there are, how many days you shoot and how closely the shots match. This guide gives you a method for sizing prop money for any scene, with the real stack sizes and prices, worked examples for common scenes and tips for stretching a small budget on an independent production. It is written for art departments, line producers and independent filmmakers. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Count the stacks the camera sees, add the hidden ones that sit behind them, double the count for any repeat set-up and add one sealed reserve. A wallet shot needs a Starter Stack, a desk spread one or two stacks, a briefcase five, and a vault ten or more. Prop money cost is driven by stack size, and orders start at $300 AUD.

## The stack sizes and prices

Every product in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) uses the same stack tiers. Sizes are described by face value, and prices are in AUD.

- Starter Stack: $1,500 face value, $115
- 1 Stack: $2,000 face value, $200
- 5 Stacks: $10,000 face value, $850
- 10 Stacks: $20,000 face value, $1,600
- 50 Stacks: $100,000 face value, $7,500
- 100 Stacks: $200,000 face value, $14,000

Orders start at $300 AUD, so a Starter Stack alone does not clear the minimum. Delivery is free from $500 AUD, and crypto payments receive a 10% discount. Prices come from the live range, so check the product page before you order.

## A five-step method

1. Break the scene into shots. List every shot that shows money: wide, medium, insert and close-up.
2. Count the visible stacks in each shot. Include stacks in the foreground and the background.
3. Add the hidden ones. Stacks behind hero bundles, under a bag or on a shelf out of focus still need to be there.
4. Allow for repeat set-ups. If the same money appears before and after a handover, you need matching stacks for both sides of the cut.
5. Add a reserve. One sealed stack is cheaper than a rush order on the morning of the shoot.

## How much for common scenes

### A wallet or hand shot

The camera sees a few notes. One Starter Stack covers it, with plenty for continuity. Spend the saved budget on a clean hero note for the close-up.

### A table spread or desk scene

A pile on a table needs volume without depth. One or two stacks give a natural-looking spread. Let notes fall loosely and vary the angles.

### A bag, briefcase or handover

A bag opening shows a thick bundle at the top. Five stacks usually fill a briefcase to the lip. Put $100 and $50 notes on the visible faces and filler beneath. If the scene shows the same bag twice, order enough matching stacks to avoid rebuilding between set-ups.

### A heist, vault or cash room

A vault is where the camera pulls back. Count the shelves, pallets and bags in the frame and work out how many bundles each holds. Ten stacks fills a modest vault. A larger set with pallets suits 50 Stacks, and a full cash room is where 100 Stacks and a wholesale conversation make sense. Read our guide to [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/) for more.

### A till or shop counter

A till drawer needs a mix of denominations and a few bundles under the tray. A Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack usually covers a till and a counter, and the combined $315 clears the order minimum.

## Prop money cost: what drives it

Prop money cost is driven by four things.

1. Stack size. The tiers above scale the price, and larger tiers lower the price per dollar of face value.
2. Denomination mix. A scene that needs $100 and $50 hero stacks plus smaller denominations for tills may need more than one product.
3. Finish. Matte, double-sided paper with consistent print costs more than a basic print.
4. Delivery and paperwork. Free from $500 AUD, and the invoice goes on your production file.

Our guide to [cheap prop money](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) explains where cheaper listings save money, and our [wholesale guide](/blog/wholesale-prop-money-for-production-companies-bulk-pricing-explained/) covers larger runs.

## Making a small budget look big

Independent productions rarely buy a full vault of hero notes. These methods stretch a small order.

1. Hero on top, filler underneath. The camera sees the top note and the edges of a stack. Put $100 notes at the visible faces and cheaper material behind.
2. Fan the notes. A fanned handful reads as a thicker stack than a flat one.
3. Vary the denominations. An all-$100 drawer looks staged. Mix in $50 and $20 notes. The [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) guide shows how.
4. Use depth of field. A shallow focus blurs bundles in the background, so they do not need to be hero quality.
5. Break the line. Open a strap, spill a few notes and leave one stack at an angle. Perfect order looks fake.
6. Reuse the same stacks. Reshoot angles with the same stacks, and move them around the set.

For a longer look at a single denomination, read [$100 prop money bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/).

## Reading the script for cash

Before the first order, read the script and the shot list for every mention of money. Mark each scene where cash appears, note whether it is held, counted, hidden or thrown, and write down how many bundles are visible. A scene that says only "he pays" needs a wallet and a few notes. A scene that says "the vault is full" needs a very different order. Doing this once, early, is the cheapest way to avoid both a thin scene and an overspend.

## Questions to ask the director and DOP

Ask before you order, not after.

1. Which shots show money, and which are close-ups?
2. Is any shot a hero insert that needs a clean note?
3. Does the same money appear in two places in the story?
4. Will the notes be handled, thrown or dropped?
5. How many takes and set-ups are planned?
6. Is there a pickup day or reshoot allowance?

The answers decide quantity, finish and how many spares you need. A ten-minute chat before the order usually saves a rush delivery later.

## Planning over several shooting days

If cash appears across several days, order the whole quantity once. The stacks match, the paperwork is one invoice and the delivery is one signature. Keep a log of which stacks went where, count them in and out each day and store them with the prop master. Our [ready stacks guide](/blog/ready-prop-money-stacks-for-fast-turnaround/) covers strapped stacks for fast resets.

## A worked budget example

Imagine a short film with three cash scenes: a bank counter, a car handover and a kitchen table. The bank counter needs a till and three hero bundles. The car handover needs a briefcase of cash. The kitchen table needs one stack in a close-up.

A practical order is 5 Stacks for the bank counter and the briefcase, which are shot on different days and can be reused, plus a Starter Stack and a 1 Stack for the kitchen table and the till. That comes to $850 plus $115 plus $200, which is $1,165 in AUD, clears the order minimum and qualifies for free delivery. Keep one stack sealed as a reserve and count them in and out on each day.

## Compliance

Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Keep the notes under the prop master's control, keep the invoice on file and never spend them. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [Reserve Bank guidance](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) for the full picture.

## Where to go next

Start with the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), see [Money Stacks](/shop/money-stacks/) for counted bundles, or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your shot list and we will suggest a quantity.

### Play Money vs Prop Money: Which One Do You Need?
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/
- Published: 2026-03-11

Pretend money and prop money look similar in a product listing, but they are made for different jobs. One is designed to look obviously unlike real currency so children can play and adults can run a game. The other is designed to read correctly on camera while staying marked and different in the hand. Buy the wrong one and you either get a shot that looks cheap or a party prop that is more realistic than it needs to be. This guide explains the difference between play money and prop money, how to choose for a game, a party, a classroom, a shoot or a stage show, what each costs and what the law cares about. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

Choose play money for games, classrooms and parties, where it should look clearly not real. Choose prop money for film, television, theatre and photography, where the money has to read as real through a lens. Prop money is always specimen-marked, printed on paper and never spendable, and play money is designed so there is no chance of confusing it with real notes.

## What play money is for

Play money, also sold as pretend money and toy money, is built for imagination and learning. Typical features:

- Bright, obviously different colours and designs. Nobody mistakes it for real currency.
- Simple, durable stock. It is meant to be handled, thrown and counted by children.
- Low cost and large quantities. A classroom or a party needs hundreds of notes.
- No attempt to match real notes. There is no need for fine print or accurate colour.

Play money suits board games, shop role-play, school fairs, fundraisers and casino-style party nights. If you only need the money to be fun and clearly pretend, it is the right choice and the lowest-risk one. Our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) include play money in packs that are clearly marked.

## What prop money is for

Prop money is reproduction currency made for scenes where the audience must believe the cash. Typical features:

- Print detail that holds up at working distance. Fine lines stay crisp through a lens.
- Colours that match the denomination on camera. Saturated golds and greens read correctly under studio light.
- Matte paper. It avoids glare. PROPPS prints on 120gsm archival paper.
- Specimen markings. Every note carries permanent markings so it is a prop, not a decoy.
- Double-sided print. A flipped or fanned stack still looks right.

Prop money suits film, television, theatre, photography and training. Browse the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) to see it.

## Side by side

- Look. Play money looks like a game. Prop money looks like cash on camera.
- Legal risk. Play money is very low. Prop money is low when it is specimen-marked and used as a prop, and it must never be spent.
- Durability. Play money is built for rough play. Prop money is built for takes and handling by actors.
- Price per note. Play money is cheaper. Prop money costs more because of print quality and paper.
- Use. Play money for games and learning. Prop money for the screen and the stage.

## How to choose for your job

### A children's game or classroom

Choose play money. It is designed for the purpose and nobody could mistake it for real currency. Our guide to [toy money and play money for kids](/blog/toy-money-and-play-money-for-kids-games-and-learning/) covers games and learning.

### A party or event

Choose play money for casino nights, fundraisers and games. If you want a more realistic look for photos, choose marked prop money and keep it out of circulation. Our [novelty money guide](/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/) explains what is safe.

### A film, TV or stage scene

Choose prop money. The camera will show the print and the colour, and a play money note will look wrong in a close-up. Read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) to size the order.

### A photo shoot or social video

Choose prop money, and read the [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) so you present it as a prop, not as real cash.

## Five buying scenarios

1. A school fair stall. A teacher needs a few hundred notes for a shop role-play. Play money is the right choice: it is cheap, obviously pretend and designed for small hands. Nobody needs fine print.

2. A casino night fundraiser. Guests will stack, bet and bank chips of play money. Bright, bold notes in several colours work well. If you want photos that look glamorous, a small stack of marked prop notes for the winners' table can be added without risk, as long as it never leaves the venue.

3. A short film with a bank scene. The camera will show a teller counting notes in close-up. Choose prop money. The detail, colour and paper are what make the scene believable, and a play money note will look like a toy.

4. A product photo shoot. The cash is a visual element in a studio. Choose matte, glare-free prop money so the highlights stay clean under strobes. Our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/) explains how.

5. A stage show. The audience is at a distance, so colour and durability matter more than fine print. Prop money is the safer choice for visual impact, while play money can work for comedic or children's productions.

## Safety and handling

Keep both types of money in the control of one person during an event or a shoot, count it in and out, and store it away from the public. Play money that is left lying around is harmless. Prop money that is left in a pocket or a bag is the kind of thing that can cause a misunderstanding. Brief everyone who will touch the notes, and keep the supplier invoice with the production file.

## What the law cares about

The Commonwealth Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at counterfeit currency and at reproductions that could deceive a reasonable person. Play money rarely raises a question because it looks nothing like real notes. Prop money is lawful when it is clearly marked, differs from genuine notes and is used for a legitimate purpose. Never spend either. Read our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [compliance page](/compliance/) for how PROPPS builds to the standard.

## What each costs

Play money is sold in large, low-cost packs because the print is simple and the paper is basic. Prop money is priced on print quality, paper weight, double-sided alignment, counting and strapping, paperwork and delivery. At PROPPS, orders start at $300 AUD and delivery is free from $500 AUD, with stacks sized from a Starter Stack up to 100 Stacks. If you only need a few hundred notes for a game, play money is far cheaper. If you need a hero stack that reads in a close-up, the extra cost buys the detail the camera sees. Our guide to [cheap prop money](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) explains the trade-offs.

## When to use both

Some jobs call for both. A film set might use play money in the background of a children's party scene and prop money for the hero stack on the kitchen table. A fundraiser might use play money for the games and marked prop notes for a photo wall. Keep them in separate containers and label them so nobody mixes them up.

## Common mistakes

- Using play money in a close-up. It will read as a toy.
- Using prop money as a party favour. It is more realistic than a party needs and may be mistaken for real money by someone who does not know the context.
- Spending either. Neither should ever be offered as payment.
- Removing markings. Do not cut, crop or cover specimen markings.
- Ordering at the last minute. Express Post is fast, but a signature is required on delivery.

## Ordering

PROPPS orders start at $300 AUD, ship by Australia Post Express with signature on delivery and are free to deliver from $500 AUD. Crypto payments receive a 10% discount. For larger runs, see the [wholesale page](/wholesale/).

## Where to go next

For games and parties, see [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/). For film, television, theatre and photography, see the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/). If you are unsure, [contact the studio](/contact/) and tell us the job.

### Where to Buy Prop Money in Australia (Legally)
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/where-to-buy-prop-money-in-australia-legally/
- Published: 2026-03-01

Search for "buy prop money Australia" and the results are a mixed bag: overseas marketplaces, unmarked novelty listings, forum posts and the occasional professional studio. Not all of it is lawful to import, carry or use on an Australian set. This guide explains where to buy prop money in Australia legally, how to compare your options, what to check before you pay and what a sensible order looks like. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

Buy marked, non-legal tender reproduction notes from an Australian business you can identify, with an ABN, a physical address, clear product descriptions and traceable delivery. That combination gives you an invoice for the production file, a local contact if something goes wrong and notes that are built to the standard in the Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) and the Reserve Bank's reproduction guidance. You can read the detail in our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/).

## Your five options for buying prop money

Most buyers end up choosing between these five routes. Each has a different risk profile.

### 1. A local prop currency studio

A specialist Australian studio is the best fit for film, television, theatre and advertising work. You get notes made for the screen, specimen markings on every note, an invoice, local support and Australia Post Express delivery. PROPPS PTY LTD works this way from Eltham, Victoria, and has supplied more than 500 Australian film, television and theatrical productions since 2019. Browse the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) to see the product.

### 2. A general prop hire house

Some hire houses stock a few bundles of stage cash. This works for a single day of theatre, but selection is limited, notes may be reused and finishes vary. It is a reasonable fallback for tiny jobs, not a plan for a series.

### 3. Party and novelty shops

Novelty and party shops sell play money that looks nothing like real currency. That is safe and suits children's games, fundraisers and classrooms, but it will not hold up in a close-up. Our guide to [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) explains where the line sits.

### 4. Overseas marketplaces

Overseas listings are where most trouble starts. Sellers often ship polymer notes that copy current Australian designs closely, with faint or no specimen markings, long delivery times and no one to contact. Parcels can be held at the border. Our comparison of [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/) goes through the differences in detail.

### 5. Making your own

Do not print your own. A home-printed copy has no safeguards, no markings and no paperwork, and a convincing copy is exactly what the law is written to catch.

## What to check before you buy

Spend five minutes on this checklist before you place an order with any seller.

1. Specimen markings. Every note should carry permanent, prominent markings. Ask for a close-up photo of the front and back of an actual note, not a render.
2. Material. Real Australian banknotes are polymer. Reproductions printed on matte paper are easy to tell apart by touch. PROPPS notes are printed double-sided on 120gsm archival paper.
3. Business details. Look for an ABN, a physical address and a working phone number. You should be able to say who you paid.
4. Honest descriptions. The product page should say the notes are non-legal tender props made for film, television, theatre, visual arts or training. Treat any claim of "government clearance", "undetectable" quality or "unmarked" delivery as a warning.
5. Delivery. Traceable shipping with a signature on delivery is the sensible standard. PROPPS ships by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with a mandatory signature.
6. Policies. A real supplier publishes shipping, refund and privacy policies and a compliance page.
7. Paperwork. You should receive an invoice you can keep on the production file.

## Why local matters

Buying from an Australian studio changes a number of small things that add up on a production:

- Speed. Express dispatch from Melbourne takes days, not weeks. A late change to the call sheet is manageable.
- Recourse. If a parcel is damaged or a count is wrong, you can ring someone.
- Paperwork. A local invoice answers questions from insurers and location owners.
- Currency fit. A local studio keeps up with changes to the real note designs, so your on-screen cash looks current.
- Lower legal risk. Local specimen-marked notes avoid the border and compliance questions that come with overseas polymer copies.

## How much to expect to pay

Prices depend on denomination, bundle size and finish. At PROPPS, orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. Notes are sold in stacks, from a Starter Stack up to 100 Stacks for large scenes. For help matching quantity to the shot, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/). If you are watching the budget, our [cheap prop money guide](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) explains where a low price usually comes from.

## A simple buying process

1. List the scenes. Write down which scenes show cash, which denominations are visible and whether any shot is a close-up.
2. Choose the denominations. Start with the [$100](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) and [$50](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) products, then add $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills and wallets.
3. Choose stack sizes. Match stack size to what the camera sees. Our guide to [$100 prop money bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) shows how.
4. Order early enough. Express dispatch is quick, but a signature is required, so plan who will be at the address.
5. File the paperwork. Keep the invoice and a note of the specimen markings with the production file.
6. Control the notes on set. Store them with the prop master and count them in and out each day.

## Buying for different uses

The right order depends on the job, and so does what you should ask the supplier.

- Film and television. You need volume, matching stacks and fast dispatch. Ask about wholesale rates if the order will repeat across a season, and keep the invoice with the production file.
- Theatre. Notes are seen from a distance, but they are handled backstage every night. Ask about durability and how many notes a run needs. Our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit lighter stage use.
- Photography. Close-ups show print detail and paper finish. Matte stock avoids glare under strobes. See our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).
- Advertising and branded content. Agencies often want a branded or custom look. Our [custom and branded props](/shop/custom-and-branded-props/) cover that, and the legal checklist still applies.
- Training and simulation. Cash-handling trainers need notes they can reuse and account for. Keep them in the training room and record their return.
- Events and parties. Marked novelty notes are enough. Keep them out of circulation and away from shops and taxis.

## Warning signs in a listing

A few phrases tell you a listing is written for the wrong reason. Be cautious of copy that promises notes which pass detection tests, describes the product as "real looking" without mentioning markings, offers discreet or unmarked delivery as a feature, or claims government clearance without linking to a document. A professional studio describes what the product is, who it is for and how it is marked. It does not need to sound like a secret.

Be equally careful with listings that hide the seller. If there is no ABN, no address, no phone number and no policies, there is nobody to hold responsible when a parcel goes missing or a count is short. Those are the same details an insurer or location owner will want to see.

## What not to do after you buy

The law is mostly concerned with what happens after the purchase. Never spend prop notes, never hand them out as tips or gifts, never cover or crop the markings in publicity stills and never post unmarked close-ups that suggest the cash is real. If someone asks about a note, show the specimen markings and the invoice. Our guide to [whether it is illegal to buy prop money](/blog/is-it-illegal-to-buy-prop-money-australia/) goes through the common situations that cause problems, and the [Reserve Bank of Australia](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

### Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 & RBA Prop Money Rules Explained for Australian Filmmakers
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/
- Published: 2026-02-15

If you are buying prop money for a shoot, a stage show or a training exercise, the law is the first thing your producer, insurer or legal team will ask about. This guide sets out the prop money Australia laws that matter in plain English, how the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) approaches reproductions of banknotes, and the practical steps an art department can take so the paperwork holds up. It is general information, not legal advice. For a specific production, check the current text of the legislation and speak to your own lawyer.

## The short answer

Making, using or passing off imitation currency as real money is a serious offence in Australia. Buying and using clearly marked reproduction notes for a legitimate production purpose is a normal part of screen, stage and photographic work. The difference comes down to four things: how the notes are marked, how they differ from genuine banknotes, how they are marketed, and what you do with them afterwards.

## What the Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at

The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) sits alongside the Criminal Code and deals with offences relating to currency. Its purpose is to protect the integrity of Australian money. In practice that means it targets counterfeit currency, and reproductions that could realistically be accepted by a reasonable person as the real thing.

Section 22 is the provision our compliance standard is built around. In summary, it is concerned with making or possessing things that look like Australian currency without a lawful basis. A reproduction that is clearly and permanently marked, and that differs from a genuine note in ways a reasonable person would notice, is treated very differently from a note that has been made to deceive. Always read the current wording of the Act on the official legislation site, because amendments happen and a blog post is never a substitute for the text.

Two points are worth stating clearly:

- The offence is about deception and misuse, not about the existence of a prop. Film, television, theatre and photography have used reproduction currency for as long as those industries have existed.
- Intent matters, but intent alone is not a defence. A prop that looks identical to a real note and is carried in a wallet is a problem regardless of what the owner meant.

## What the RBA says about reproductions

The [Reserve Bank of Australia](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) is responsible for Australian banknotes and publishes guidance on reproducing banknote images. The guidance exists because banknotes carry security features, and because convincing copies cause real problems for shops, banks and the public. The RBA's position, in broad terms, is that reproductions must be clearly distinguishable from genuine notes, for example through changes in size, one-sided printing, or prominent markings, and must not be used in a way that could mislead.

The RBA updates its guidance when new banknote series are released, so check its banknote pages before you finalise a brief. If your production needs something the standard guidance does not cover, such as a close-up hero shot of a new-series note, the RBA is the body to ask, and the answer should go on your production file.

## How PROPPS builds notes to the standard

Every product PROPPS PTY LTD sells is a non-legal tender reproduction prop made solely for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. We have been supplying Australian productions from Eltham, Victoria since 2019, and more than 500 film, television and theatrical productions have used our work. The compliance standard behind every note is simple:

1. Specimen markings on every note. Each note carries permanent specimen markings so that no one could mistake it for legal tender at a glance or in the hand.
2. Paper, not polymer. Genuine Australian banknotes are printed on polymer. Our notes are printed on non-reflective archival paper, so the feel is different the moment someone picks one up.
3. Deliberate differences from a genuine note. We design reproductions to deviate from the real thing in material and treatment, not just in a label.
4. Honest marketing. We never describe prop notes as spendable, undetectable or interchangeable with real money. Our pages say what the product is and what it is for.
5. Traceable dispatch. Orders ship by Australia Post Express with a mandatory signature on delivery, so every parcel has a named recipient.

You can read the same standard on our [compliance page](/compliance/), which is the page to send to a producer or insurer who wants it in one place.

## A compliance checklist for productions

Use this list when you brief the art department or prepare a production file. It takes about ten minutes and answers most of the questions an insurer or location owner will raise.

1. Name the purpose of the notes in the call sheet or prop schedule, for example "reproduction currency for scene 14, bank counter".
2. Keep a copy of the supplier's invoice and the specimen marking details on the production file.
3. Store prop notes with the prop master or art department, not loose in a costume pocket or a personal bag.
4. Brief the cast and background performers: the notes are for the camera and they are never spent, shown off or posted as real cash.
5. If you shoot in a public place, tell the venue or local police beforehand, and keep a copy of the supplier details on set.
6. Return, destroy or securely store unused notes at wrap. Do not leave them in a location or hire car.
7. Keep close-up hero shots of any note under your own control and check the RBA's current guidance before you publish stills or trailers.

## Red flags when you choose a supplier

Prop currency is sold by a mix of professional studios and anonymous sellers. A few signals should make you stop and ask questions:

- Claims of "government clearance", "RBA approved" or "100% compliant" with no source. Regulators do not hand out approvals for individual prop sellers. If a claim has no link to a document, treat it as a sales line.
- Language about passing detection tests. Anything that suggests the notes could fool a pen, a scanner or a cashier is describing the wrong product.
- Discreet or unmarked shipping offered as a feature. Legitimate props do not need to hide. Traceable, signed-for delivery is the safer arrangement for everyone.
- No Australian business details. An ABN, a physical address and a contact number are the minimum. You should be able to confirm who you are paying.
- Overseas listings of polymer notes that closely copy current Australian notes. These sit much closer to the legal line and can be held up at the border.

For more on weighing up local and overseas options, see our guide to [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/).

## Using prop money on set and in public

Most compliance problems happen after the camera stops, not in the shot. A few habits prevent them:

- Do not hand prop notes to anyone outside the production, including as a joke or a tip.
- Do not use them at a shop, ATM, taxi or vending machine, even as a test.
- Do not post unmarked close-ups to social media with captions implying the cash is real.
- Do not leave notes visible in a parked car on location.
- If a member of the public or an officer asks, show the specimen markings and the supplier invoice. That is what they are for.

## Special cases

Content creators and advertising. The same rules apply to a social media video as to a feature film. If the clip is meant to look like a real cash giveaway, the risk is the presentation, not the prop. Read our guide to [prop money for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/).

Training and simulation. Banks, retailers and security trainers use reproduction notes for cash-handling exercises. Keep the notes in the training room and record their return.

Theatre. Stage use is low risk because the audience is at a distance, but backstage handling still needs control. Our [theatre-friendly range](/shop/event-and-party-props/) is built for that.

## Where to go next

If you want specimen-marked notes that your legal team can sign off, start with the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), compare the [$100](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) and [$50](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) products, or read our guides on [whether it is illegal to buy prop money](/blog/is-it-illegal-to-buy-prop-money-australia/) and [the legal difference between fake money and prop money](/blog/fake-money-vs-prop-money-the-legal-difference-in-australia/). Orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500, and crypto payments receive a 10% discount.

### How Cinematographers Light Prop Money on Camera to Eliminate Glare
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/
- Published: 2026-01-20

Cash is one of the hardest props to light. It is small, it is printed in fine detail, it is often handled by an actor in a close-up, and the paper reflects light in ways that a script supervisor will never notice but a lens always will. Realistic prop money can look flat, shiny or fake purely because of how it was lit, even when the notes themselves are excellent. This guide is written for directors of photography, gaffers and art departments. It covers what makes notes catch light, how to place the key and fill, how to test before the day, and the handling habits that keep a stack looking right across a long shoot. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Use soft, large, angled light, keep reflections off the lens axis, test the exact notes under the exact lights at working distance, and choose matte paper so there is less glare to fight in the first place. If a note shows a hot spot in your test, change the angle of the light before you change the note.

## Why prop money reads badly on camera

Three things go wrong most often.

- Specular glare. A glossy or lightly coated stock acts like a small mirror. A single hard source produces a bright patch that hides the print and flags the note as a prop.
- Flat, even lighting. A bank of diffused fill from the front removes the subtle shadows between notes in a stack. A stack then reads as a single block of paper rather than a bundle of notes.
- Wrong colour balance. Banknote inks are saturated. Mixed colour temperatures, for example a tungsten practical beside a daylight window, push the greens and golds in different directions and the cash stops matching the rest of the frame.

Realistic prop money starts with the paper. PROPPS notes are printed double-sided on 120gsm matte archival paper, which removes most specular glare before a light is switched on. That is a deliberate choice for the camera, and it is also why the notes are easy to tell apart from genuine polymer notes by touch.

## Choosing the light

### Soft and large

A large soft source close to the subject wraps around a stack and keeps highlights gentle. A softbox, a bounced source or a window with diffusion all work. A small hard source is the quickest way to create a hot spot.

### Angle it off the lens axis

Reflections follow the angle of incidence. Place the key so that light striking the note bounces away from the camera, not into it. A useful starting point is to put the key at roughly 45 degrees to the table and to the side of the camera, then adjust while watching the monitor.

### Use negative fill to keep the print dark where it should be

Banknote print is detailed. Too much fill lifts the shadows and flattens the engraving. A black flag or a dark card opposite the key restores depth and makes the stack read as three-dimensional.

### Keep practicals honest

If a lamp in the frame is warm, match the key to it or gel the key. Cash looks wrong when the colour of the light on the notes does not match the colour of the light on the actor.

## Close-ups, inserts and hero notes

A hero note for an insert needs more care than a stack in the background.

1. Choose the cleanest, flattest note from the order and keep it separate from the working stock.
2. Light it on a table first, with the camera at the planned lens height, before the actor's hand is in the shot.
3. Check both sides, because many scenes flip or fan notes. PROPPS prints both sides to the same standard.
4. Keep fingerprints off the surface. Oil from the skin picks up as shine under a low angle.
5. Replace the hero note after a few takes. Handling softens the corners and the camera will see it.

## Stacks, bundles and the money shot

A stack has to look like many notes, not one. Light from the side so the edges of the notes show as fine lines, and let a little shadow fall between bundles. For a vault or a table spread, treat the money as a texture: raking light shows the layers, while flat frontal light hides them. Our guide to [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) explains how many stacks the camera actually sees, which saves you lighting more than you need to.

Use hero stacks of $100 and $50 notes in the foreground, because their colours read strongly, and mix in smaller denominations for tills and wallets. The [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) guide shows how to choose.

## A five-minute test before the shoot

Run this test on the day before, or at the start of the call.

1. Set up the actual lights, flags and practicals for the scene.
2. Place the notes where they will sit, at the planned height.
3. Look through the lens or on the monitor at the planned distance for wide, medium and close.
4. Tilt the stack slowly and watch for hot spots.
5. Fan a note and flip it, as the actor will.
6. Photograph it on the camera you will use and check the result on the monitor, not on a phone.
7. Adjust the light, not the notes, until the print reads cleanly.

## Lenses, cameras and sensor differences

A long lens compresses a stack and exaggerates the effect of a single reflection, while a wide lens shows more of the table and more of the light stand reflections. Shooting at a high resolution reveals paper grain and print detail that a lower resolution hides, so test at the delivery resolution. If you shoot on a camera with limited dynamic range, keep the highlights on the notes under control, because a clipped highlight on a white border cannot be recovered. A fast lens at a shallow depth of field softens background stacks, which lets you spend less on them.

## Colour and exposure tips

- Expose for skin and let the notes fall where they fall. Cash that is brighter than the face pulls the eye away from the actor.
- Keep the notes within one stop of the surface they sit on, so they do not glow.
- If you are shooting a green or gold dominant frame, check that the note colours are not being absorbed into the background.
- Match colour temperature across the frame and avoid mixed sources on the cash.
- If you use a polariser, test it. A polariser can cut reflections, but it can also change the apparent saturation of the print.

## Handling and continuity

Realistic prop money only keeps looking realistic if it is handled with care. Store the notes flat, dry and out of direct heat, because paper that has been in a hot car curls at the edges and catches light differently. Keep a spare stack sealed. Use gloves for hero notes. For repeated takes, rotate the stock so the same notes are not handled every time. For ageing and weathering, read our [art department guide](/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/).

## Compliance on set

Lighting a note so it looks real is part of the job, but the notes must stay clearly marked props. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender reproduction for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Never spend them or present them as real cash in publicity material. The [Reserve Bank](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions, and our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains the standard.

## Where to go next

See how the notes look in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/), compare the print quality in our [guide to judging high quality prop money](/blog/high-quality-prop-money-how-to-judge-it-on-camera/), or [contact the studio](/contact/) with your lighting setup and we will help you choose.

### The Art Department Guide: Weathering Prop Cash for Underworld Realism
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/
- Published: 2025-11-10

Brand-new notes straight from the box rarely look right on screen. Real cash has been in pockets, bags, drawers and tills. It has creases, a little grime on the edges and a slight curl. An art department that dresses prop cash for sale on screen has to decide how worn each stack should be, how to keep the wear consistent across takes and how to avoid damaging the notes that need to stay clean for the hero shot. This guide is written for prop masters, art directors and set decorators. It covers weathering and ageing methods that are safe for paper notes, continuity rules, how to plan hero and background stock, and the compliance habits that protect the production. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Age the background, protect the hero, and keep a log. Weather a limited number of stacks to a consistent standard, keep a clean reserve for close-ups and for reshoots, and record what you did so the next day of shooting matches. Never age a note in a way that removes or covers its specimen markings.

## Why weathering matters

Cash tells the audience who a character is. A freshly strapped bundle on a mobster's table says something different from a roll of soft, creased notes in a market stallholder's apron. The details the camera sees are the top note, the edges of a stack and the way a note bends when it is counted. Getting those right makes a scene look lived in without anyone noticing why.

## What the camera sees

Before you weather anything, work out what will be seen.

- Top note and edges. These are the parts that carry the story. A stack is a surface and a side, not a block of paper.
- Hands. When an actor counts or fans notes, the notes bend, and the camera picks up creases and corners.
- Depth. In a wide shot, a bundle of notes in the background reads as colour and shape. It does not need the same treatment as the hero stack.

That is why a prop master rarely weathers every note. Weather the notes that will be handled and seen, and leave the rest clean.

## Weathering methods that work on paper notes

PROPPS notes are printed on matte archival paper, which takes light weathering well. These methods are common in art departments. Always test on a spare note first.

1. Handling and rolling. Fold, crease and roll the notes by hand. This is the safest and most natural method and it keeps the print intact.
2. Light edge toning. A dry tea or coffee wash, applied sparingly with a cloth, adds warmth to the edges. Let it dry fully before stacking.
3. Dry dust and grime. A fine, dry pigment on the edges mimics the dirt that gathers in a till. Seal nothing and keep it light.
4. Corner softening. Rub the corners gently with fine paper to round them off. Real notes round at the corners first.
5. Bundling and strapping wear. Leave a strapped stack in place for a day so the strap leaves a faint line, and the stack gains a slight memory of its shape.

Avoid anything that obscures the printed specimen markings, anything wet enough to curl the paper permanently and anything that could stain a hero note you still need clean.

## Plan hero stock and background stock

A simple way to organise a scene is to split the cash into three groups.

- Hero notes. Clean, flat and handled as little as possible. These are for inserts and close-ups. Keep a spare.
- Working stock. Lightly weathered notes for hands, drawers and counting.
- Background stock. Strapped stacks and bundles used for volume. Matching stacks keep continuity simple. Our [ready prop money stacks](/blog/ready-prop-money-stacks-for-fast-turnaround/) arrive counted and strapped for this.

Tag the groups so no one swaps a hero note into the working pile. For how many stacks to order, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/).

## Continuity rules

Cash scenes are shot in pieces, often over several days, so continuity is the main risk.

1. Photograph the stack before the first take, from the angles the camera uses.
2. Weather in batches. Treat the whole quantity for a scene at the same time, so it matches.
3. Log the process. Note the method, the date and the quantity. A reshoot a month later will need it.
4. Count in and out. Count the notes at the start and end of each day. This is good practice for continuity and for compliance.
5. Keep a sealed reserve. A clean spare lets you replace a damaged hero note without a rush order.

## A weathering workflow for a one-day shoot

When there is only one day, keep the process short and repeatable.

1. Morning before call: weather the working stock by hand. Roll, crease and soften corners on the notes that will be counted or fanned.
2. At the first set-up: photograph a hero stack and a working stack from the camera angle, and tag them.
3. Between set-ups: reset stacks from the same batch, not from new stock. Swap in clean notes only for the hero insert.
4. At lunch: check the working stock for damage and replace anything torn.
5. At wrap: count, bag and label the notes, and write down what was used.

## Common weathering mistakes

- Over-ageing. Notes that look filthy read as costume jewellery. Real cash is mostly just soft.
- Ageing everything. The background does not need it and the clean notes are your safety net.
- Wet methods that curl the paper. Curl does not reverse and the camera will see it.
- Skipping the log. A reshoot without a record means guessing what the notes looked like.
- Covering the markings. Never age a note in a way that hides its specimen markings.

## Stage and theatre use

Theatre cash is seen from a distance and handled nightly, so it needs to survive repeated use rather than look perfectly aged. Choose durable notes, weather lightly and expect to replace stock during a run. The same count-in, count-out habit applies backstage. Our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit lighter stage use.

## Period and set dressing details

Period work adds another layer. A scene set decades ago may need older-looking notes, different bundle styles and different wear patterns. Talk to the set decorator about what the character would plausibly carry, and match the wear to the setting: soft, folded notes in a worn wallet, crisp strapped bundles from a bank, loose notes in a tin. Small touches such as a rubber band, a paper clip or a folded receipt make a stack read as belonging to a person rather than to a props department.

Think about the end of the scene too. When the shoot wraps, decide what happens to the weathered notes: keep them as a ready set for a pickup day, retire them, or return them to the studio. Weathered notes cannot be made new again, so label the box clearly and keep the log with it.

## Directing the cash scene

Directors use cash to shape a scene: a bag of notes opened slowly, a stack slid across a table, a till drawer that is almost empty. Talk to the art department early about what the camera will see, how the money moves and how many takes there will be. The answers decide how many stacks to buy and how much to weather. If you shoot a reveal, such as a vault or a briefcase of cash, read our guide to [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/).

## Compliance while you work

Weathering is a creative step, but the notes are still reproductions. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender prop for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Keep the markings visible, keep the notes under the prop master's control, keep the invoice on file and never spend them. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the full standard.
